subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, March 10, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Ilsley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Blackmore, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon during this debate, which is the only opportunity we have aside from the war approriation bill, I proceeded to say a few words about the conduct of the war. As you know, sir, in the parliament at Westminster ninety-five per cent of the time is taken up with war measures.
I agree with what has been said, that there is no such thing as home defence in this country. Norway found that out; Denmark found it out; Holland, Belgium and France found it out. All their home defence amounted to nothing against these mechanized hordes, and the same is true of all the occupied countries of Europe. We shall find out the same thing if they come here. We shall find that the way to fight our enemy is to fight him on the seven seas wherever we can find him. The First Lord of the Admiralty (Mr. Alexander), referred in London yesterday to the battle of the Atlantic and the submarine peril along the same lines as what I said here yesterday.
I may say that first Germany relied on her air arm in attacking shipping, and on a secret weapon, Hitler's magnetic mine. That continued for the first year and a half of war. It did not prove a success, as was expected, and the enemy then turned to the submarine, which had proved so disastrous to the allies in the last war. Germany accordingly went in for the building of larger and improved submarines in an effort to defeat Britain at sea and starve Britain. That submarine campaign has been a great success so far for Germany, and unless the allies solve this problem the war cannot be won.
Notwithstanding the brilliant advances made by General Montgomery, General Alexander and General Anderson in the Libya campaign,

where the enemy was chased for fourteen or fifteen hundred miles-and that was really our first success in the war-the battle of the Atlantic cannot be won without the allies, especially Britain, the United States and Russia, gaining command at sea. Germany's submarine campaign, under skilful direction, ' is now to attack allied shipping at long range from their advance submarine bases in Norway and the bay of Biscay and we shall have to have more escort ships to protect our convoys in the Atlantic against these attacks. In 1940 we received fifty old destroyers from the United States, which were a great help in our convoy system then, but we need still more escorts to win the battle of the Atlantic. I referred yesterday to 120 escort ships we cannot get back from the North African Armada. The situation is grave, as the First Lord of the Admiralty said. I recall the time when he was a pacifist, just a few years ago. Before the war he was in favour of reducing the number of our capital ships from seventy-five to fifty and was responsible for changing at the Washington conference the definition of a capital ship and for preventing the building of more and rearmament. Sometimes chickens come home to roost, and that applies to the pacifists in the old country as well as to those in the dominions who supported complete disarmament. Some of my friends to my left were wrong. They relied on pacifism and disarmament before the war. That was their blueprint. A few also wanted to reduce the estimates for the armed services to the sum of one dollar. The result was that when the war broke out practically all we had to rely on if attacked, as I said before the war, was the girl guides, the boy scouts and the honorary colonels.
I believe the time has come when we should discard politics. The winning of the war is all that matters. We had politics in this parliament for four months in 1942. We had a long debate on Bill No. 80 and time taken up with a referendum and all that kind of thing, and the war was only secondary. The war situation this year is too serious for that. There are many domestic problems of great magnitude and importance that affect our mode of living, but the war is primary and the rest are secondary, and must await a later day. As General Sir Bernard Montgomery said in January, 1943:
If each one of us, whether front line soldier or officer or man whose duty is performed in some other sphere, puts his whole heart and soul into this next contest, then nothing can stop us. Nothing has stopped us since the battle of Egypt began October 23, nothing can stop us now. We will all be in the hunt eventually:

The Budget-Mr. Church
on to Tripoli. Our families and friends in the home countries will be proud when they hear we have captured this place.
It wras a 1400-mile British advance in Libya not an Anglo-American advance. Canada did not congratulate those brave generals of our own; another novice ambassador though, has congratulated another allied general on his successes in the east. I contend that we should also congratulate our own people, and give them equality of treatment.
In connection with the budget I wish to say a few -words, I am sorry the minister is not in his place. I cannot agree with the glorious company and the hallelujah chorus and the brass bands and the hip-hip-hurrahs about a five billion dollar budget for this country. The situation is too grave for all these mansions of finance in the sky. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is one of the pacifists-one of many in all parties-responsible for this gigantic budget. They thought we could make peace pacts, protocols and paper and disarmament agreements and be protected, when they well knew the situation. The minister himself went to the league of nations the year before, to this talk-fest in Geneva; he must have known that a disarmed Britain just meant invasion and insult and in the end extinction. The pacifists in and out of the house must shoulder some of the responsibility for this gigantic expenditure. I doubt if the money is being well spent, these astronomical figures; when you get up in the sky five or six miles the money is less likely to be well spent than a moderate sum would be. When I go back home I see the retailers and wholesalers who pay the taxes, and the working classes of this country, and remember that they have already committed themselves on mortgages and agreements for sale of land and small houses and fire and life insurance. In Toronto the assessment commissioner's report used to show that fifty-five to sixty per cent of the people owned their own homes, because Toronto is a city of the middle classes and the toilers and workers of this country. My friends to my left have not been unmindful of the condition of these people, nor have the Conservatives who sat in this house, because they have been the friends of labour and their policies for many years past have been for the benefit of labour.
Do not forget that Canada is the highest taxed country in the world. The minister talks about the United States and Britain, but in the United States there is no sales tax; here there is a sales tax on almost everything, even coal and on everything used
in the kitchen. I do not care whether the stand I take, that of saying they are taking too much money from the people, is popular or not, but the people back home know more than the people in Ottawa. They are complaining and trying to find ways and means of paying these new forms of taxes. They do not object to paying taxes for the war, but in this budget we find many millions not for the war at all; look at the increase of civilian estimates. What is the use of establishing embassies across all the seven seas in time of war? Are those things necessary? Do they contribute anything to the war or defence on the home front? These novice ambassadors are bad in peace time but more dangerous in war time. You can go over many of the other items in the estimates and find the same sort of thing. Not a man or woman in Canada objects to what is necessary for war purposes; the government can go the limit to win the war, but when you find a lot that is not for war you do complain. Notwithstanding all that was said about the four freedoms and all this kind of thing, we are going to be a desperately poor people after this war.
We have squandered our resources at a great pace. We are spending money like water and wasting our national resources and the products of the sea, the soil, the forest and the mine. I have here a return for four years before the war, showing the quantities of base metals supplied by us to our enemies- copper, platinum, nickel, some sixteen of them. You allowed these people to get all those natural resources from us and by reason of the policy of isolation on the part of our great ally to the south our enemies, the Germans and Italians, built a navy in the Atlantic.
A civil war was fought in England for nearly a hundred years to gain control of the exchequer, but to-day this house has lost that control; with all the controllers and subcontrollers we are the forgotten agency of government. So much is this so that we were in session last year five months to the first week of July and never discussed one item of the estimates, there was so much politics in connection with our discussions in 1942. This budget shows no attempt to put on the brakes. Alexander Mackenzie sat on the strong box and we had an auditor general named McDougall who had power to veto expenditure. That proviso has been taken away now from the auditor general, and the budget from first to last shows the dead hand of the treasury and no authority and absolute failure to check all this expenditure. Too much money altogether is being taken out
The Budget-Mr. Church

of the taxpayer and too much is charged to income and not enough to capital. This generation is suffering in flesh and blood, and future generations should pay also.
The last war was said to be to make the world safe for democracy. When the troops come home from this war they will find that this war was fought to make the world safe for bureaucrats, Donald Gordon and all his regiments and colonels and lieutenants wearing the epaulettes of this whole control system, part of which is necessary but which is overdone, and some of the people not able to get a bit of beef, butter or sugar. There are pictures in all the papers of this commander-in-chief of the bureaucratic forces waving his ration book, and pictures of his sisters and his cousins and his aunts and all his family and of his inability to get butter at his club while parliament sits here, the forgotten agency.
I have a letter here from the auditor general, a good official, Mr. Watson Sellar. I asked him what power of veto he has over expenditure. He has none. He replied to the extent of two pages, and he points out that under the appropriation bill there is a comptroller of the treasury who has little control, and that there is a two billion dollar war appropriation which he can do nothing about; parliament only authorized it in a few sentences, without any items being given. Why did we authorize it? When parliament passes a blanket appropriation bill we lose all control over it. What have the war expenditure committee ever done? They took a Cook's tour of Canada accompanied by Mr. Togo and they were stuck in some of the fog at the head of the lakes. They divided into subcommittees to investigate technical problems and where is their report? What did they find out? Not a thing to put the brakes on. They have divided themselves into subcommittees to investigate a great many technical problems about which they know no more than the average county councillor, or perhaps not one-tenth as much. If we had in our municipal systems the antiquated federal practice in force here, I believe the tax rate would be a great deal higher in local systems because these municipal councils know how to stop a great many of such unnecessary expenditures. The auditor general might just as well be said to have no control; for every controller is his own auditor and there is no head to the whole thing. We are getting to be a nation of auditors, and we have so many of these controllers that they do not know what they are supposed to control. Take the question of potatoes. We were told over the radio that there was a great shortage of potatoes, but now we are told that the situation is not nearly as bad as we supposed. I had a letter from a 
prominent public man in Toronto the other day in this regard, telling me that his wife heard over the radio that potatoes were scarce and everyone should put some in. I wrote the wartime prices and trade board in this regard and had a letter back from the young gentleman who is now secretary of tile board and who seems to have great influence with the government, since he goes from one federal job to another. Mr. Fowler said that in a letter he had received from a member of the advisory committee for potatoes in Toronto he was given this information:
Let me inform you that preseent short supplies are not as serious as many would declare. Moving along such streets as Bloor street, St. Clair, Jane and Annette streets in Toronto, all stores have potatoes for sale, mostly in ten and fifteen pound packages.
Then he adds that seventy-five pound bags are also available in some stores if desired. This is a conflict of rival people, all contradictory on the matter of potatoes, and small potatoes publicity people.
There is one thing we shall have to do before the soldiers come back. There has been too much bullying of the public in this country by the wartime prices and trade board. It should be called the wartime tower of Babel board, with all the lectures it gives the people and its male and female announcers, or the wartime prices and farce board. What do some of these unpractical, young people know about business practices? One young man was appointed "to simplify practices in small businesses connected with clothing." He ordered the cuffs taken off trousers, narrower collars, and so on. Where was he employed before he undertook to tell the retail storekeepers,. all their life in the retail trade, what to do? He was working in a well known brewery; and there was no scarcity of beer at that time That is the sort of control we have here. Dio Mr. Donald Gordon have any training in any competitive business? He did not. Does he know anything about butter, coffee, tea or beef? All the butter, potatoes, beef and coffee he ever saw were what he consumed himself; yet he is placed in authority over the wholesalers and retailers of this country. It would have been far better to have the control of our food supplies with the food men in the business. I agree with the statement made the other day in a land of plenty by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that rumours have caused rationing. I think we should have followed England's lead and left these matters under the control of those who have looked after them all their lives, business men who are actually in business, instead of appointing a great many highbrows; because you have to

The Budget-Mr. Church
be a highbrow to get a job as a controller or subcontroller, while the "real men" are serving at the front. Not long ago when I was going into the union station in Toronto I saw a young fellow in uniform, a soldier, on the right of way tracks, who was shovelling snow for the Canadian National Railways. He had been a teller in a bank. He did not enlist to shovel snow; he enlisted to fight Hitler.
In my opinion the people will stand for whatever is really necessary in the way of regimentation for actual war, but they will not stand for anything they do not feel is absolutely justified and will not help one iota for war purposes. If we do not do something about it the people will do something about us. Why, they have a small standing army of prosecutors, investigators and enforcement officers peeping through keyholes to see whether blackouts are being observed, and all that sort of thing, though in England blackouts have been largely eliminated as the right hon. the Home Secretary said, curtailed and further regulated. I have complained about the matter of the length and frequency of these blackouts in central Canada for two years to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), under whose authority these blackouts are held, because that authority is delegated to other people over whom there is no control. The people who are in charge of these blackouts are good, patriotic people; they are law-abiding, patriotic citizens doing a great public service, voluntarily, but I believe it would be far better if they were in the reserve army or getting better results in other form of war work, doing something that would be of more practical value to the people of this country. I appreciate the fact that in my own city many public-spirited men and women have done a great deal of good work in this connection, but I believe they could be given better and more valuable war work to do in these times. You cannot beat Hitler by turning a light on and off. In Norway and Finland everyone was taught to handle a rifle, and I think that should be done here. Then we have all these hundreds of advertisements printed in both languages in an English-speaking province. Why is that necessary in the English-speaking province of Ontario? It is just a waste of money. I ask hon. members from the province of Quebec if they think -money should be wasted in that way. I say it is not necessary, and all this duplication should be stopped.
If it is necessary to ration tea, coffee, sugar and butter, why should there be all this talk about it? No one will object if it is necessary, but when you find one agency saying one thing over the radio and other agencies saying 72537-74
other things in the press and in interviews and speeches, it is a different matter. If we had left the distribution of these commodities to the food industry in Canada who understand it, we would be far better off. No doubt there would have been some difficulties, but I think we would have had greater food reserves if that had been done. As a prominent man, a great economist, in England, Lord Perry, said not long ago:
A completely socialized Britain would mean that all power was vested in the permanent officials. A free-enterprise Britain, such as our fathers and grandfathers knew and upon which our national prosperity rests, means that bureaucratic power is severely limited. Therefore, the further Britain is taken from free enterprise and the nearer she is brought to state ownership, the more complete is the power of the bureaucrat.
Let it be emphasized that whatever new fields of government the bureaucrat commands, he does not add to his responsibility. That is still borne by the political ministers whom he directs, whom he tutors and whom he paralyses. The natural trend, then, of a political minister's professional advisers is toward legislation which gives wide scope to the department which launches it. It is this thirst for power which inspires that type of legislation which Lord Hewart in his "The New Despotism" found so objectionable-legislation which leaves departments free to lay down rules and to impose regulations against which there is no appeal either to the courts of law or to parliament itself.
In this budget there is little comfort for the small retail dealer or wholesaler or toiler who has been put out of business by some of these controls. Then, as I say, I do object to the cost of it, because last year I asked the minister what the cost of this pegging ceiling policy was, and he did not know. At Easter-time of 1942 Mr. Gordon made a speech in Winnipeg in which he said it was $2,000,000. Later the minister made a statement in the house corroborating that figure. At the end of last session, in a return brought down at my request, $50,000,000 was the amount stated for this control. I do object to some of the big-stick bullying tactics used when dealing with the public. They are unnecessary in Canada, because our people are progressive, law-abiding and willing to do anything that is necessary for the winning of the war.
Many poor labouring people have suffered because of a coal famine brought about by a lot of useless orders and failure to see ahead. Credits were curtailed by order No. 225 of the wartime prices and trade board. The result was that these people had to pay the amounts owing by the 25th of the month. The coal dealers were not complaining; we have a fine patriotic lot on the whole in Toronto; they were willing to extend credit

The Budget-Mr. Church

to their customers, some of whom had bought from the same firms for fifty years. In some instances two generations had dealt with the same coal companies, but the coal dealers could not send coal to a poor customer who might have been out of work and could not pay cash, or to a home in which a soldier's family may have lived. They could not get a ton of coal without paying for it before the 25th of the month, or cash on delivery. This absurd order brought about untold privation and suffering among the poor and was legislation against human nature.
Last session I urged, and I urge again at this session, that there be a fixed date for the presentation of the budget. I ask again that a ways and means committee be set up to deal- with matters contained in the budget. The budget now before us is copied from Washington.
I have in my hand the annual review of the National City Bank of New York, issued in February of this year. It deals with the United States President's address in which he transmitted to congress his hundred billion dollar budget for 1944. From this publication I read the following quotation:
In transmitting to congress the new budget of over $100 billions for the fiscal year 1944 the President referred to the budget presented a year ago as "An instrument for transforming a peace economy to a war economy."
The present budget, he said "presents the maximum programme for waging war."
In the United States they have reached their maximum. What is our objective? We hear it said that it is five billions of dollars. I venture to say there will be a deficit of two billion dollars before this year is over. And with a further deficit on current account and on civilian estimates we do not know where we are going to land. There are practical business men in the house who could serve on a committee. On some of the committees now sitting here the work is being done by able business men, capable of giving sane advise to the ministry instead of a number of teachers, former teachers, former professors and some highbrows. For these reasons I recommend the setting up of a ways and means committee, to go over the budget first.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in keeping with many other hon. members who have spoken in this debate I wish first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon the splendid presentation of the fifth war-time budget. The task of a minister of finance in peace time is heavy, indeed; but the task in war time is much heavier and more onerous. I say

without fear of successful contradiction that the minister wTho has just brought down the fifth war-time budget ranks high in comparison with ministers of finance who have preceded him; and in my opinion his ability in the house as Minister of Finance has not been excelled.
The magnitude of the war is not yet fully realized by many people in Canada. In this connection I am reminded of a sign I noticed when, as a member of the war expenditures committee, we visited the Curtiss aeroplane plant in Buffalo, New York. It read thus:
Never in all human history have so many people known so little about so much.
Before dealing with the matters under my hand I should like to say a word or two respecting the remarks of the hon. member . for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Mackenzie), who spoke in the debate yesterday afternoon. He had many suggestions to make, and made several criticisms respecting what takes place in the house. With much of what he said I agree, but I do take exception to his suggestion that we cut down to twenty minutes the speeches of hon. members, and I take further exception to his deprecating speeches made generally in the house. It is true that we might do without many of the speeches; many of them are perhaps not worth while sending home. But after all, a member of parliament has a duty to perform. His is the only voice in parliament speaking for the people he represents. If he sits on the government side and remains silent, he does more harm, I believe, to our democracy than do members on the opposition side, and some few on the government benches, who make criticisms as well as suggestions. If free speech is ever curtailed in the house it might be, in my opinion, the beginning of the curtailment of free speech outside the house. The right given to every hon. member to speak freely and as often and long as he likes in parliament, distasteful as it may be to some, is still a great safeguard and bulwark of democracy, and grievances must be sometimes aired in the House of Commons.
I compliment the minister upon bringing down the pay-as-you-earn plan. By some it has been called the Ruml plan, and the other evening the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) described it as the Ilsley plan. To my mind the Minister of Finance need make no apology for the plan he has presented. True, it does not go as far as many had expected, because, as we pointed out in a recent issue of the Ottawa Journal, many people had an idea it would do away with much of our taxes. At least this much can be said about it, that through its minister

The Budget

Mr. Reid
of finance the government has adopted the principle of the Ruml plan. I find it amusing to note that Mr. Ruml is still travelling the length and breadth of this country, lecturing the Canadian people about the Ruml plan, despite the fact, as I learned in the press a short time ago, that the plan as enunciated by him has been definitely turned down by the people of his own country. I am reminded of speeches made up until 1939 about peace in this country when we did not have even a gun to defend ourselves-a fact we have regretted since.
Our views have changed somewhat in the last few years. While the government is not going as far in matters of finance as many of us would like it to go, still the minister should be complimented upon moving forward-some might say to the left. At least in his speech he did leave the impression he was fully aware of what had been proposed by many of us in days, past, and what we still propose, that what is physically possible is financially possible. When he spoke about the $983,000,000 he had had to borrow from the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks I was glad he admitted the dangers in these borrowings. May I point out to him that before the war ends he may well have to consider the issuing of national funds or loans from the Bank of Canada, because we are not yet through with the war. When one realizes that our deficit this year will be $2,899 million, that on top of that- the Canadian banks hold in securities well over two billion dollars, and that our dominion debt is close to eight billion dollars, making a total national debt of eleven and a half billion, one is startled by the figures of debt. One must stop to consider these mounting debts. We wonder where it will end. If the minister cannot obtain all the money from the people of Canada, the problem is indeed a serious one. I for one would like to see him give further consideration to dealing more, in some controlled way if he must, with the Bank of Canada. It is not for lack of savings, because we should realize that over three billion dollars have been contributed by the Canadian people through the purchase of war savings certificates and bonds since the war commenced. The number of bank accounts has increased since 1939, as well as the number of depositors. I was glad to hear the minister comment favourably upon the voluntary work done by the war savings committees and those handling the sale of war bonds. I want to add my meed of commendation to those willing workers who helped put this over. The minister referred also to the thousands of citizens who have been redeeming their
5M37- 74*
bonds. To me that is a serious thing because, as the minister pointed out, the redemption of bonds weakens the home front, and we cannot afford to allow any front to be weak in this war.
The minister spoke also of price control. It is not my purpose this afternoon to deal with the prices board. I have dealt with it before and I shall deal with it at a later stage of the session. But he said that while there had been criticism of the wartime prices board, no one had yet seen fit to suggest its elimination. I may say to him that if no one has seen fit to do that it is because many of our people are afraid that if they did so they might be called unpatriotic. In my travelling back and forth across this country I find that there is a growing storm of protest which has been kept down only by the patriotism of our people. It may well break out at the end of hostilities.
I know there will be those who will contradict what I am going to say now, but it is my opinion that no great trouble was encountered during the last war because prices and wages rose. I am not advocating that there should be no control; I am simply pointing out to the house that it was not until well after the war, when the collapse of the boom had taken place, that any tragedies occurred, if there were tragedies. I think we should have a far-sighted policy. I am just wondering whether the people of this country will be ready to permit the wartime prices and trade board to operate as it has been since its inception, especially when the thought is in the minds of many of our people, particularly our merchants, that large business is consolidating its position during this time, to the detriment of the individual merchant.
In the debate last year I brought up the matter of the position of the Canadian 'and the United States dollar, and asked the Minister of Finance for a statement as to why our dollar should not be at par with the United States dollar. I pointed out to him that the definite statement had been made officially in the United States that the fact that the Canadian dollar was ten per cent under that of the United States was due entirely to the request of the Canadian government. Personally I cannot understand, when we are all allies in this fight, when we are trading under lend-lease and every other kind of trade arrangement, when we are pooling our forces, why we should be called upon to pay ten per cent more for a United States dollar than we should have to pay.
According to the latest trade returns, the premium on United States funds cost Canada $45,000,000 extra for the goods we bought
The Budget-Mr. Reid

in the United States last year; since the wat commenced we have paid more than $150,000,000 extra because our Canadian dollar was at a discount. I am going to ask the minister now, and I shall ask him again when we are in committee, to explain why the Canadian dollar should not be on a par with that of the United States.
The minister told us that there would be tax increases on essential and non-essential goods. Additional taxes have been placed on cigarettes, tobacco, wines and spirits. Some may argue that these are essential goods, and others will argue that they are not. I am not going to take up the time of the house this afternoon by entering into a debate of that kind. But I do ask the government to give some consideration to the motion picture industry of this country.
Let me say at the outset that I realize that motion picture theatres play a big part in our lives. I appreciate also the difficulties faced by many of the smaller theatres in our small towns. It may interest the house to know that there are only some eleven theatres in Canada that charge fifty cents and upwards for admission. The lowest charge is fifteen cents. There has been a considerable increase in the number of admissions. Almost all our citizens are gainfully employed and enormous numbers are working in factories. They have crowded into our cities, and everywhere we see long queues in front of the theatres, especially those in Ottawa. One wonders whether a small tax could not be placed on these theatres. After all, the war must be financed, and I am of the opinion that this tax would not keep one single person from entering a picture theatre. I am sure that no great protest would be raised when the people realized that the money being taken from them by way of tax was for war purposes. I leave this thought with the minister and the government for further consideration.

I am not sure whether that
information is in this bulletin. Most of the information regarding pictures is given, but I do not think it gives the amount of money sent out of the country. I have read it from one end to the other. I shall endeavour to find out and let my hon. friend know.
Another matter I want to touch upon is one which has been referred to by many hon. members in debate, both this session and last session. I refer to the Old Age Pensions Act. In the estimates this year is an item of $400,000 for pensions for war widows. I am sure this announcement will be well received throughout the country, and I commend the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) for taking this action. I should like to say a word or two about old age pensioners and the effect that the present low amount of pension is having upon some of them.
Some members from the middle provinces and the east may get a little impatient with our representations in connection with social legislation, especially old age pensions. Let me point out to them that the western provinces have led the way in social legislation. Had it not been for the lead of the western provinces I doubt if old age pensions would now be paid in some of the provinces. I say that without fear of successful contradiction. Some credit therefore is due to the western provinces, especially British Columbia, for giving that lead. The old age pension association, I believe, sent a resolution to the government. I am not going to read the entire text; copies went to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of Labour. Amongst other suggestions they asked that the age limit be reduced, and that the amount be increased to $30. They asked

The Budget-Mr. Reid
that the regulations be amended-and something in that respect should be done without delay. They asked that the value of the home should not be taken into consideration unless it is worth more than $3,500. They asked also that the residence clause be amended, and particularly, that the regulations be stripped of all features which tend to reduce the pensioner to a pauper of the state.
I could read to this house many letters which I have received, and no doubt many other hon. members are in the same position, and I shall cite only one case to show how the regulations affect some of our people. It is the case of a man who had two sons in the services and whose cheque was withheld by the department at Ottawa. When eventually it was paid it came too late, for the old age pensioner had died. Not content with that, the department followed the matter up with a request that a deduction of seven days be made on the ground that the man had died two days before Christmas. I think every hon. member will agree that that was going a little too far. That is what often happens with members of the finance control sitting in Ottawa with a blue pencil, looking over accounts which come in. Everyone must be incensed at incidents of this kind of callous treatment. I urge upon the government first of all that the regulations be amended and revised from a more humane point of view; also that until the matter has been dealt with by the committee on social security the government should at least match the allowance of five dollars which is now being paid by the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta. As you know, those two provinces are giving five dollars extra to all old age pensioners and calling it a cost-of-living bonus. The cost-of-living bonus given by the dominion government is greater in most instances than the entire amount allowed to old age pensioners. Remember that actions speak louder than words; and when we are speaking of a new era after the war, and thinking of the gallant young men and women who have offered their lives, one wonders how they will regard all this kind of talk if no practical steps are taken, especially in behalf of our aged citizens.
I shall now deal for a few minutes with another matter which has been brought up in the course of this debate; it was mentioned by the Minister of Finance on March 2, when, speaking about tariffs, he said, as reported in Hansard, page 861:
The customs tariff has fallen from the high position it has previously held as an instrument of fiscal and economic policy. Under the circumstances of war, the tariff has little effect except as a producer of revenue.
He said further:
There will again, however, be a time when the tariff will be an important instrument of trade policy and when this country will have to decide whether it will play its part with other countries which are prepared to help in freeing the world's trade, in enlarging markets, and in promoting the full and effective use of the world's resources.
The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) also mentioned the subject. He took the stand in his address that nothing should be done now in connection with the tariff, that it should not be disturbed, and that no approach should be made to the United States or any other country until the war is over. I differ entirely from the view held by the hon. member for Danforth, because it is my belief that if we wait until the end of the war and a depression sets in, at least until industry can change over, there will be little hope of ever reducing the tariff protection given to the manufacturers of this country, and there certainly will be no hope that United States manufacturers will be willing even to discuss tariff reductions, let alone change their attitude. Now is the time that the approach should be made looking towards world free trade as referred to in the speech of the Minister of Finance.
The other evening the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), speaking in the debate on social security, referred to private industry.

We talk of the new order 1 If we cannot fix up our own house I wonder just how we are going to lead the world in free trade. Only a few days ago a small aluminum plant in Vancouver was compelled to close down. It employed twenty-five experienced men and could easily use seventy-five. That plant had been going for twenty-five or thirty years. But it was shut down, and all the aluminum we need now comes from the east. The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation referred to the large aluminum companies; I trust that some improvement will be made in the industrial conditions in British Columbia. One suspects that behind all this there is some hand operating to prevent us from getting what we believe to be fair treatment in the matter of industries. Now is the time that changes should be made.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) in his address to the house, the other day wondered what was going to happen to his city after the war. I can tell him. British Columbia and Nova Scotia both have a blackout now, and after the war the same thing is going to happen to Nova Scotia as to British Columbia-we are going to have an economic blackout if the matters mentioned are not remedied.
I wish to speak of another matter which has been brought up at every session I have attended when the Ottawa agreement bill, under which the dominion government pays $100,000 to the city of Ottawa, comes up for discussion. I mention particularly the city of Ottawa, but my purpose is to draw the attention of the house and the government to the seriousness of the problem of tax-free crown lands in cities and districts all across this country. The situation is becoming very serious, and Ottawa is just one example. The total assessment of the city of Ottawa is in round figures $162,000,000, and the assessment

The Budget-Mr. Gillis
of tax-free government property is this year
S61,500,000.	The loss in taxes to the city of Ottawa through the government taking over this property will be $2,345,322 in actual cash in 1943. You might think that Ottawa was about the worst case in the dominion, but it will surprise many members to know that it is not. We have districts in British Columbia where the situation is even worse. In Esquimalt eighty per cent of the total assessed property in the municipality is tax-free government or crown property. I have another case where the percentage is ninety, and if I had time I would give the complete figures. In Coquitlam the total assessment is roughly $7,500,000, and the tax-free government property is $6,200,000; in other words ninety per cent of the total assessment is exempt from taxation. Another ten per cent and the government will own the whole municipality! Vancouver's loss in taxes this year through tax-free government property is $1,270,778. Ten per cent of the total assessment is tax-free government property. In my own city of New Westminster the loss in taxation from this same cause is $27,000. One could go on from city to city. I merely cite these instances to bring them to the attention of the government and to ask that something be done about it.
The Alaska highway was mentioned the other evening by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) when he was speaking of airfields and highways through Canada to Alaska. First of all I wish to compliment General O'Connor and his staff of United States officers upon having done a splendid job there. But I am going to suggest to the government that even though the United States is putting up the money for the highway, this government should have some say as to the route. The present route connecting the airfields almost by-passes the whole province of British Columbia. Dominion engineers some years ago had made extensive surveys and laid out two routes designated as A and B, which go through country far superior to that traversed by the present route. If any member thinks that the new Alcan highway is going to develop northern British Columbia, he had better investigate a little further. From the information I have, it runs through the poorest kind of country. The country through which the two other routes run is far superior. Moreover, the Alcan highway has grades of twenty per cent, while routes A and B, as laid out by dominion government engineers, have grades of less than one per cent. Canada should take some definite stand in this matter. We should not just let the United States engineers go in there and have all the say as to the route.
We are looking for great developments after this war; we shall require good land on which to settle many of the returned men who may want to go on the land. I ask the government to take note of what is taking place in that part of the country, and I would point out to the United States authorities and their engineers that any future route should be one of the routes which we ourselves have already laid out. The present route will not develop our northern British Columbia country as it should be developed.
My time is up, Mr. Speaker, and I shall have to leave until a later occasion many other matters on which I wished to speak.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) in paying tribute to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon his presentation of the budget to the house. He made a very fine speech, and I have just this further observation to make in connection with it-that it would make one of the best election speeches I have .ever heard. The speech from the throne itself would also make an excellent election manifesto.
I realize the position of the Minister of Finance in working out the budget that he has just presented to the house. He has one of the most difficult jobs in Canada, and he is doing it as well as anyone in the country could do it so long as the rules of the game are what they are. His job during this war is to keep the present capitalist economy in balance, and he has done an excellent job so far, with a lot of assistance, of course, behind the scenes from those who are interested in no other order of society but the one we have. In view of the fact that there is practically no change in the rates of taxation in this budget, it is quite clear that the Minister of Finance and his advisers recognize that they have gone as far as they can with respect to taxation under the present rules of the game. I am afraid that if the war lasts another two or three years, and if we are successfully to carry out our part in it, fundamental changes will have to be made with respect to the bases of society in this country. This budget is a clear indication of that.
The house now has something definite to discuss. The Progressive Conservative party must regard it as satisfactory, in view of the fact that they have not proposed any amendment to it. They are satisfied that it should be our guide or yardstick until the next budget is presented. The Social Credit party has proposed an amendment; the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group have proposed an amendment to the amendment, and
The Budget-Mr. Gillis

I shall try to relate my remarks to the subject matter now being discussed as closely els possible.
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group decided after scrutinizing the amendment of the Social Credit party that it was necessary to move an amendment to the amendment, because we could not see that the Social Credit amendment proposed any basic changes as far as our economic system is concerned. We believe that if changes are not made along the lines proposed by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment we shall not be able to weather the storm that we see ahead.
We are fearful of the growth of monopoly in Canada, and it is on that point that I wish to dwell this afternoon. We realize that those who are interested in private enterprise, as they call it, and a smaller concentration of the direction of private enterprise in the hands of a smaller group than has had it during all our lifetime, certainly are not supporting what will build a democratic order of society. What I shall endeavour to show this afternoon is concrete evidence of that development. I do not question the sincerity of members of the government who are bringing in measures and appointing committees with respect to social security, advocating old age pensions and allowances of all kinds and setting up committees to do research and bring in recommendations with respect to social changes after the war. What we are fearful of now is that the group who control are away ahead of the government in their post-war plans. I see to-day in Canada through the manipulation of industry and finance, and the concentration of that manipulation in the hands of fewer and fewer people, the laying of the plans now for what we are going to have in the aftermath of the war. All these committees represent one point of view and one only. All the recommendations are along certain lines. They are building an order of society now that means complete control by themselves after the war. I do not make that statement for the purpose of creating unrest; I believe it is an actual fact.
I know that the boys in the army are fighting for social changes. None of them wants to come back to what we had. I cannot see any of those who have had the administration of affairs by manipulating the economic resources of the country, who have done the job that private enterprise under that particular control has done during the past twenty-five or thirty years, making changes in the social order that prevailed prior to the outbreak of the war. In my opinion they are building a machine that will guarantee control 
by themselves after the war. Through the medium of our war boards you have the heads of the large corporations sitting in and taking advantage of the seriousness of the war situation and the necessity for production. The large corporations are sitting in on the boards now and not only planning the war effort but utilizing the plants created by the government and routing them into the economy of the country so that when the war is over they will own them; also setting them up to their own advantage, as they have certain arrangements with respect to writing off the money put in by the government. The thing is so arranged that when the war is over they will own and control these plants. We have example after example right across the country. The wartime prices and trade board have authority to close out some twenty thousand non-essential industries, and they are doing it step by step in the different provinces. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) a moment ago referred to the closing of a war plant, an aluminum plant, in his section. Production is concentrated in some plant in central Canada, centralizing control in the hands of one small group. This is not an isolated instance; it is taking place all across the country.
Another example is the malleable iron works in Oshawa, a plant employing some 125 men. I have had letters in recent weeks concerning it. This plant has been and will be in the future necessary to that community, and its closing will be a loss to that community. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) no doubt will try to find employment for those men elsewhere; nevertheless in taking the plant from that community the men are being scattered across the country and their homes broken up. The significant feature is set out in the following paragraph:
The O.M.I. plant used to do a lot of work for McKinnon Industries, St. Catharines. The orders were pulled out by McKinnon and now McKinnon has a request for men to go to St. Catharines. We were once told by heads of selective service that they would bring the jobs to the men and not the men to the jobs.
McKinnon Industries in St. Catharines is a fairly large organization, and it was handling the work from this smaller plant. Now with its priorities it is in a position to close out the little plant and take the employees to St. Catharines to work for them there. This malleable iron works was on war work, making a definite contribution to the war effort, and it was necessary to that community. The men who worked there will have to leave that section and go elsewhere and their homes will be broken up. I do not think there is any justification for actions of that kind. It is an

The Budget-Mr. GiUis
indication of monopoly control gradually closing the smaller industries out of the picture.
Only last summer I had this experience in Ontario. After speaking at a meeting one night a man came to me and introduced himself as the manager and part owner of a plant in that section. He employed some eight hundred men. He said, "I want to have a talk with you. Could you send over to my plant an organizer from steel workers to organize my plant?" I replied, "Well, that is a peculiar request to come from the owner and manager of a plant. What is the catch?" "There is no catch at all," he said. "We find ourselves in this position: a small industry not linked up with the large corporations who now control the field through the medium of the war boards and the priorities boards. We cannot get priorities on materials, and as a result our business is shrinking so that unless something is done within the next year or so we shall be completely closed up. This business means something to this community; it has been here for many years, and the only way we see to secure redress is by allowing our employees to organize in a union, link themselves up with the legitimate congresses in Canada, and have them make the necessary fight to keep this plant in operation."
That is the situation in these smaller plants, and those are only two examples. That was why we thought it necessary to place this amendment before the house. I do not expect my words to change anyone's vote, but those hon. members who listen and understand the reasons for these things but are not prepared to do anything about them will have to take the responsibility in the aftermath of the war, when the situation I am now describing will be so solidly established that we will not have a chance of changing it. Then with respect to exemption from taxes, we find the Minister of Finance announcing that the lumber industry of British Columbia is to be granted a tax exemption privilege.

For every thousand board feet of timber produced, the operator's taxable income will be reduced by $1; and for every thousand feet in excess of the 1941 cut, another dollar may be deducted. income tax on approximately $2,500,000 of income. This measure, in Mr. Ilsley's words, is designed to encourage production of lumber. speechtext:
Not according to this article. This would lead me to believe that they were deliberately curtailing operations, in other words going on a slow-down strike. I thought I should place that on record, because I have listened to the miners being hauled over the coals because they were looking for enough to eat, not to mention any exemption from taxes. My object in mentioning this matter and putting it on record is to show that there is not equality of sacrifice.
There is another matter I think we should thoroughly understand, one in which every hon. member should be interested; for after all, regardless of the party to which we belong, each must satisfy his own mind in regard to these things. We are all Canadian citizens and we represent Canadian citizens, and we shall have to take our full share of the responsibility for the conditions that prevail after the war. These matters should be looked into and efforts made to correct them. I refer now to the system followed by the government with respect to the setting up of new plants, the creation of crown emanations. I hold in my hand the summary of an agreement between the government and Norwegian Canadian Packers Limited under the War Exchange Conservation Act, dated March 4, 1943. This is a new company that has been formed; apparently to-day the name "Norwegian" is popular. I believe this is a fish packing plant which is to be set up in the province of New Brunswick. A special depreciation allowance has been fixed against plant expenditures of $105,000. The plant is located
The Budget-Mr. Gillis

at Cham cook, New Brunswick, and the government has allowed the company a special deduction based on export sales of a maximum of 880,000 which may be written off in the three years 1943, 1944 and 1945. I interested myself in this matter because I believe the government is making very generous provisions in regard to the establishment of this company, and I know that so far as the fishermen of New Brunswick are concerned the greatest efforts that have been put forth looking to their rehabilitation have been made by the extension department of St. Francis Xavier university of Nova Scotia, which went in there for the purpose of organizing and educating the fishermen of that province, to assist them toward a solution of their own problems. I believe this Norwegian Canadian Packers Limited is a combine from some other part of Canada which sees the possibility of the fishermen of New Brunswick being taken out of the hands of the private fish buyers, and as a result the elimination of a great deal of exploitation. I believe the company is cutting in there now, while we are in the process of fighting this war, in order to bring the fishermen of New Brunswick back under the wing of the private fish buyers. If that assumption is not correct I want somebody to correct it when he has had time to check up.
This is a further development of the monopoly which is spreading across Canada from section to section. To-day we find Canada Packers interested in other things than the processing of meat. They are not standing still; they are planning, too, and from coast to coast they are entering other fields than meat packing; chickens, chicken farms, dairies and so on. They are not planning their production or distribution for war purposes; they are cutting in and consolidating their position now in order to be sure of holding the whip hand when the war is over. Only this morning I had a letter from an individual in Nova Scotia who is very much interested in the development of cooperatives. While I am on that point let me say that as far as I am concerned I visualize the future of Canada from the point of view of cooperation. Any economic system in this country must be based upon the principle that the people will have a major say in its development, on the basis set out by the extension movement in Nova Scotia to which I have referred. It seems to me that any economy based on any other principle can only move in the direction of the order of society against which we are fighting to-day overseas. It cannot go anywhere else. This order of society, in the opinion of men who have studied it and who 
are speaking and writing on it, can extend in only one way, the way Hitler represents in Europe, the way he is fighting to foist on the rest of the world. Unless the people themselves get together and organize the economic processes of the country, have a say in the marketing and in all phases necessary to the life of the people, we shall have lost the very objectives for which we are fighting the war.
I said a moment ago that from one end of Canada to the other Canada Packers are moving in, doing their own organizing and laying their own post-war plans. Not only are they laying them, but they are actually putting them into operation. Let me read one paragraph from a letter:
Here in Nova Scotia there are some interesting stories about farmers who through group action, that is cooperation, organize to do their own business. In the Annapolis valley the creameries are nearly all in the hands of private operators-there is only one little cooperative. Last year these creameries paid five cents a pound less for butter fat than the farmers were getting in northwestern Nova Scotia where the great Scotsburn cooperative creamery is the yard-stick for the price. Five cents a pound on butter fat means that a farmer who has ten cows pays a toll to these operators of $12 a month, or $144 a year. It can easily be seen that this extra tax from one hundred farmers is a tidy little sum over and above the regular returns of the business. In other parts of Nova Scotia the private creameries paid last year seven cents a pound less for butter fat than was received by the farmers of the Pietou, Cumberland, and Colchester areas, where the cooperative creamery sets the price.
This paragraph brings to our attention the fact that in that section Canada Packers moved in last summer and endeavoured to buy up the privately-owned creameries. Had it not been for the fact that the cooperatives stuck together and recognized the trend of events, protecting the farmers from taking any action, Canada Packers would have full control of the distribution of milk.
I believe every hon. member should be raising his voice against the lack of representation on boards from the average ordinary citizens of the country. On boards which are now planning I note a complete absence of the rank and file of our people. For instance, in connection with the distribution of food we might have called in representatives from the cooperatives and have given them an opportunity of sitting on boards. Regardless of what anyone's opinion may be about Canada Packers, and with all due respect to the men who have been selected, I say that no man is in a better position to sit on a board set up for the purpose of arranging for the marketing and distribution of foodstuffs than a man who has spent the last twelve or fifteen years working among the people, organizing and per-

The Budget-Mr. Gillis
fecting his organization. Nevertheless we do not see any of those people consulted. They are not represented; they are passed by. I note that on the new fuel control board there have been appointed a lawyer from Halifax, the head of the Bank of Canada, and another king's counsel from Quebec. These are the men who head up the fuel control policy in Canada. I have no doubt that in their own fields these men are experts, but when the government is endeavouring to lay down a fuel control policy for Canada it might select men who have had a closer connection with the problem. There is no doubt that this is a big job, because distribution of any product in Canada is difficult. We know that. I do say, however, that on that board there should be men who, through the medium of their organizations, represent the workers. These are men who for the past twenty-five years have made a road to Ottawa, presenting brief after brief to the government on the question of the development of a national fuel policy. Surely they should be called in and given a place on the board, to attain a solution of the problem-that is, if anyone honestly wants a solution. Sometimes I wonder if the whole machine is not designed to create confusion and chaos, and to keep control within the hands of a certain small group. The average citizen who might get in on these boards might learn too much. That is my honest opinion as to why they are not taken in. They might see too much or find out too much, and they might expose manipulations to the people.
I have heard it stated by many hon. members that we must set up some kind of machinery for the distribution of foodstuffs. Whether it would require the establishment of another ministry is a matter entirely in the hands of the government, but some machinery will have to be perfected to see to it that essential commodities are properly distributed across Canada, so that they may reach the working people who are slaving in the plants and factories in order to make our war effort a success.
I raise this point this afternoon because in the last few weeks I have received many telegrams and letters from Nova Scotia respecting shortages of essential foodstuffs. Let me now pay my respects to the editor of the Ottawa Citizen. I have some respect for the average newspaper editor. I believe many of them have a lot of common sense, and at least they try to keep informed of matters they are writing about. But in this instance the editor of the Ottawa Citizen in his comments was neither fair nor informed respecting the rationing of foodstuffs in Nova Scotia. First he belittles the miners in their
gesture to the government to get the necessary rations, and then he creates the impression that there was only a shortage of butter in the area. He played up the suggestion that there had been a threatened strike because of the butter shortage. He goes on to point out that the miners were looking for rations greater than those of the average citizen in Canada.
A newspaper editor, who is responsible to a great extent for the moulding of public opinion, should check his facts more closely than apparently the editor of the Ottawa Citizen did in this instance. That shortage was not temporary. It was not something which developed overnight. It was not a shortage of butter only. The fact is that it was a shortage of practically every commodity. Seven weeks ago I was on the island of Cape Breton. I know that servicing on the island, so far as food1 is concerned, is done through the medium of cooperative stores in the mining areas. While on the island I visited two or three of the stores and noted that the shelves were practically empty. On a Saturday evening I had a conversation with the manager of one of those stores, which catered to about two thousand people, and he pointed out they had practically no butter, and that there was no meat to be sold-bacon, ham or beef. The only meat which could be had was fowl. One could buy chickens, but he would have to pay a fancy price. That condition had prevailed for some time. There was no substitute for butter. One could not buy jam, syrup, or anything of the kind. In short there was a scarcity of every commodity.
For the benefit of the Ottawa Citizen and its manager, may I point out that the percentage of enlistments both in this war and in the last one from among the miners in that area was the highest of any point in Canada.

To be fair to the
miners, is it not so that two of the largest locals repudiated the idea of a strike?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but the Ottawa Citizen did not. It created the impression throughout central Canada that the miners of Nova Scotia were proposing to go on strike because of a shortage of butter, or because they
The Budget-Mr. Gillis

wanted a larger ration of butter than that granted to anyone else in Canada. Such was not the case. I am ready to take the editor of the Ottawa Citizen to Nova Scotia and I will ask him to assume the responsibility of maintaining a family of four children while working as a miner. The editor of the Ottawa Citizen appears to be a great believer in private enterprise and all those things, but I think I am safe in saying that if he sticks out the life of a miner and accepts his obligations for one month, he will come back to Ottawa a communist.
The thought I want to leave with members of the house is that there is no one on the north American continent who works as hard as the coal miner. He must be fed, and fed properly, otherwise he cannot do the work. He gets out of bed at five o'clock in the morning and drops down a shaft a thousand feet deep to go out six miles under the Atlantic ocean. You do not work as the average man works; you must strip yourself to your shoes and overalls. You have to live practically on a can of tea. There is no sunshine and you practically sweat blood. You arrive home at five o'clock in the evening so tired that you cannot even read the newspaper. That is the life the miner is obliged to lead 365 days in the year. These are the conditions that exist at present and have existed practically all of my lifetime. There is nothing to look forward to except the breadline, and the chances are that you have not too long to live. If you stick it out and are an extra good worker you may be able to meet your legitimate obligations at the end of the week. But you must be fed, and well fed.
There is a shortage of every kind of commodity and has been for some considerable time. I think the situation is sufficiently serious to warrant the government's taking hold of it immediately. There is no shortage of foodstuffs in Canada.

I discussed the matter with the Minister of Finance and was given the assurance that everything possible was being done. That was early this week, but I received a telegram only this afternoon giving a list of the commodities which are short.

If extra rations have been sent in, apparently that fact has not seeped through to these people. Last summer there was a shortage of butter in Toronto. This was sufficiently serious to make the civic authorities talk about setting up their own rationing programme. In my opinion butter was drawn from other sections of the country and sent into that section in order to quiet the holler that was being made. The result was that a shortage was created somewhere else.
Only a couple of weeks ago Toronto was advertising the fact that there was a surplus of butter in that section of the country and they wanted the ration increased. According to the Ottawa Journal of this morning, butter production is up 27-6 per cent in February of this year as compared with February, 1942. There was not a serious shortage of butter in February, 1942, and if production has increased 27-6 per cent, there should be no shortage of butter now. I am not going to read the press clippings from all sections of the country, but I have gathered them together because I am interested in this matter. In different parts of western Canada and Ontario the plea has been made by the farmers that they should be permitted to market their surpluses of butter.
As I said a moment ago, it is a matter of distribution. I do not think a committee going down there to look into the situation, especially when it has been shown that there is a shortage, is going to remedy things. The fact is that the president of the district organization of the united mine workers has given warnings of these shortages from time to time to the wartime prices and trade board, and representations have also been made by the heads of the cooperative societies.
What should have been done was to determine in what sections butter was available and to ration on that basis. There should be sectional organizations to handle the distribution and marketing in the different provinces according to what is available and the requirements of the people. This complaint comes not only from the miners but from people in every class of society in Nova Scotia. Evidently there is a real shortage of foodstuffs. I hope that the government are doing something about it. If they are, apparently the word has not got through yet.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) make the announcement while the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Koebuck) was speaking that provision had been made for the payment of pensions under the War Veterans' Allowance Act as recommended by the last parliamen-

The Budget-Mr. Graham*
tary committee on pensions. I got the impression that this matter would be taken care of immediately, but in checking the thing over I find that the present position is that the estimates contain an item of $400,000 to provide for the payment of allowances to the widows of members of the armed forces in the last war. It seems that this cannot be made operative until after the estimates are brought forward. What the minister should have done was to have an order in council passed authorizing the payment of these allowances, pending the estimates being brought forward. I suppose like myself every hon. member has been receiving letters from widows of ex-soldiers pointing out that the minister had made this declaration and asking just when and how the pension was to be paid. In asking around I find that it may be a couple of months before the estimates are brought down.
There are two or three other matters I should like to mention to the minister but I notice that Mr. Speaker is getting restless and I suppose I shall have to defer them to another day. I ask hon. members to consider and check my remarks this afternoon with respect to the development of monopolistic control in Canada. With all due respect to the committees which have been appointed to work out programmes for social change, I am of the belief that those in control, those who have been in control for the past seventy-five years and who hold the purse strings behind the scenes, are not only making their own plans but are putting them into operation and will offset anything we have in mind unless parliament is prepared to accept its full responsibility and protect the people from the developments that are taking place.

-and that is true of a great many generalizations made by members of his particular group, if I may say so. All the people of Canada, with the exception of a few who are profiting thereby, are a unit in opposition to the growth of monopoly. We do not need to argue about that. But I suggest to my hon. friend that we have learned a great deal about the matter of monopoly by incorporated companies. I would recall that the joint stock company as we now know it, a useful adjunct if properly used in the conduct of the nation's business, is of comparatively recent origin. As with all types of new entities, it has taken the democratic process, and particularly our legislative assemblies, some time to discover and realize some of the abuses which may attend the use of that particular entity, the corporate set-up; but I suggest to the hon. member, recalling what has taken place in the United States, Great Britain and our own land, that we now know some of the dangers of abuse through a study of the operations of joint stock companies, and that it is an easy matter, now that we understand them, to correct any evils, not only evils of monopoly but any others which may accompany the growth of what otherwise is a fairly useful instrument in the conduct of the business of this country.
I ask my hon. friend to consider the attitude he takes. What he proposes as a cure for a situation which we all agree must not exist is to remove the paramount authority, namely, the government or a free parliament, which is always there to control all such evils and has the power to do so. If you concentrate those industrial agencies in an organization clothed with all the powers of a government, there is neither a court of appeal nor any other authority above that particular instrument. We would be the unwisest people on earth to give to any group, government or otherwise, complete control of the business agencies of this country, because then we would in very truth be creating a monopoly without any
The Budget-Mr. Graham

power to destroy that monopoly if it functioned against our interest. That is a point we must not forget.
I find, and I say this with deference, a certain fuzziness of mind in the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group as to what their, policy means. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), a very able representative of the farming community of my province, makes the mistake of thinking that his party is identified with the growth of cooperative enterprise. Let me say to him that I am at least a sincere friend and proponent of cooperative enterprise. In our own province it has shown more growth than in any other province of this dominion or any state of the United States of America. But the truth is that if you adopt socialism, or centre the industry of this country under government control, you do away with the need of cooperative enterprise. Cooperative enterprise knows that; its leaders in this country are well aware of it. The use of the word "cooperative" in the name of the party which the hon. member supports is a misnomer if he wishes to apply it to the type of cooperative enterprise that he and I support.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South, speaking the other day at Hamilton or some other eastern point, suggested that during war time the government now in power has taken unto itself by order in council so much power that it is almost in the position of a totalitarian authority. I think he described it as state-ism.
