I return to what led me to rise and speak in this debate, and I hope I shall be able to make a more constructive contribution on this subject than on what has

The Budget-Mr. Graham
occupied my time so far. I speak on it because of a certain portion of the budget address of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and because I attach to it the greatest possible importance. I believe the time has now come when we, as the governing body of this country, in surveying the present and the near future must spend considerable time in appreciating the importance of the fiscal policy which this country proposes to carry through, not only in the days of the war, but in the very difficult post-war days.
We have heard a great deal in this house, and quite properly, about rehabilitation, reconstruction. reestablishment, social security and all those other subjects that are more or less allied to our intention to better the economic position of all the people of Canada. I think one thing all of us will agree we must do, even in approaching these most important social measures, is to see to it that they are needed as little as possible. Some of our young men when they come back from this war may want to adopt the army life as their career; but the vast majority of the young men who come back when victory is won will be farmers, lawyers, working men, merchants and other civilians who have been torn out of their civilian life and called to the country's service in the armed forces; and in discussing measures of reestablishment we must always keep that in mind. I can readily recall, as can every other veteran in the house, that when we came back from France after the last war at least ninety per cent of the men in uniform had one desire and one desire only, and that was to get out of uniform and back into their civilian careers as quickly as possible. It will be a regrettable necessity if we have to pay to large numbers of men now in the navy, the army and the air force their pay and allowances for any extended period after the war, but we may have to do so. While that may satisfy their immediate needs it certainly will not satisfy their mental and spiritual desires. We must make of Canada a country that will absorb their efforts in the vocations they want to follow. In that way, and in that way only, can we find a satisfactory solution of the problems in which we are all so vitally interested and of which we are a unit in attempting to find a worth-while solution.
What truths have been emphasized by this war? One of them is the interdependence of nations one upon the other, and that the welfare of one has a relationship to the welfare of the other. If that is true in the international field, it is also true that the welfare of the people of Saskatchewan is of importance to the people of Ontario, and the
same with regard to every other territorial economic unit in this dominion of ours. Then let us apply the wise principles which we so often quote with regard to charity. Let us apply these wise principles of interdependence to our own country and then extend them to the other countries of the world.
Another truth that has been emphasized by the war is a keener realization of the place of money in our economic life. We now know that the total annual national income is best expressed in the total of the goods and services produced or acquired by all of the people of the country, and that the standard of living of an individual is determined by his securing for himself an equitable and reasonable portion of that total annual national income of goods and services. Obviously, therefore, any fiscal policy, if it is a wise one upon which to lay the foundation upon which we are to build this .better life which we all desire so much, will be one that seeks to create the greatest possible annual national income. Then we must see to it that that largest possible total is distributed so far as is humanly possible equitably and fairly among all the people of this dominion. These should be the general aims of a wise fiscal policy.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) pointed out on Tuesday night a very striking truth, namely, that during the war we have spent some twelve and a half billion dollars and that that total equals one-half the total accumulated assets of Canada in 1933. He drew certain conclusions from that. I would draw another. He and his group, as I have understood them in this house, have frequently said that we should in some way take hold of that accumulated wealth, without paying interest or any reward to the persons who accumulated that wealth. We, on our part, have attempted to point out the very great relative importance of our annual production of wealth expressed as I explained in the earlier portion of my remarks. The very statement made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar illustrates more clearly than I was able to do the relative unimportance of the accumulated wealth of this country as compared with the importance of the annual national income that Canada is capable of producing. Our annual national income is that which we should safeguard, and we should increase and encourage it so that there will be a greater total to distribute among the Canadian people.
Saskatchewan, in the Sirois report, by the late Hon. Norman Rogers, a man most highly respected and honoured in this country, by
The Budget-Mr. Graham

many other economists, and by all hon. members from that province, has been pictured as the orphan in our economic family. We say there is a measure of truth in that. Like the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), I regret the stories told in this house of individual cases, because I do not believe their recital by some hon. members properly describes the magnificent people we have in Saskatchewan. You know, Mr. Speaker, how diligently we who come from that province have struggled to get for its people a certain measure of equality in the governmental and departmental policies adopted for the government of this country. But I feel certain that I speak for the vast majority of the people of that province when I say that we would readily surrender all of the bonuses and benefits that we have received by way of compensation from the federal treasury, or what are sometimes described as hand-outs from the federal treasury, if we could secure an equality of opportunity for the people of that province to produce the goods they can, and to find the most advantageous market at reasonable prices for their products, and in turn to buy whatever they require in the cheapest and best markets of the world. That is the gift I would wish the Liberal party to give to the people of my province, because that would put them in the position of that honest dependence on their own efforts which every free British citizen so much desires.
If that is the case, I think, in view of the statement by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, it is necessary that we get to these fundamentals in the remaking of this country. I wish to repeat his statement; it is not lengthy and on account of its importance I should like it to appear again and again on the records of this house. I should also like to see the same sentiments uttered by members of parliament from the central provinces of this great dominion. The statement to which I refer is as follows:
There will again, however, be a time when the tariff will be an important instrument of trade policy and when this country will have to decide whether it will play its part with other countries which are prepared to help in freeing the world's trade, in enlarging markets, and in promoting the full and effective use of the world's resources.
The government has already, by an exchange of notes with the United States on November 30 last, undertaken to enter into conversations with that country-
If I may interject, I heartily congratulate the government upon that particular step.
-and with other countries, for the purpose of formulating programmes of agreed action directed to the expansion, after the war, of production, employment, and the exchange and
[Mr. Graham.1
consumption of goods, to the elimination of all forms of discriminatory treatment in international commerce and to the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers.
I am happy indeed to note that the government feels committed to these projects.
Committed to these objects and having in mind particularly the vital concern of this country in access to the selling and buying markets of the world, the government is prepared to discuss with the government of the United States, the government of the United Kingdom, or the governments of other countries with which we trade, reciprocal trade arrangements wider in scope and longer in duration than have hitherto been made, provided always that the advantages of such arrangements shall be open to other countries willing to adhere to the same terms.
We believe that questions of post-war commercial policy must be tackled broadly and boldly; we believe that world trade must have a more liberal and dependable charter than it has had in the past two decades; and that countries, such as Canada, for which world trade is the very blood stream, should be prepared, not merely to accept desirable arrangements but to take the initiative in working out a plan mutually of benefit to ourselves and to other countries. We believe that countries, which have had long experience of friendly relations should associate themselves with that initiative and furnish to others examples of concrete accomplishment in the distribution of the world's products for the mutual welfare of all people.
That, I say again, if it is meant-and I make no suggestion that it is not fully meant by the Minister of Finance or the government of which he forms a very important part- is a very important pronouncement of policy by this government and one to which I hope to give every assistance in carrying to fruition, the fullest fruition possible, because I believe it means the greatest prosperity for this country in which we are all so vitally interested.

speechtext:
A little late,
is it not?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Better late than never. I want to deal with that phase of this question. The Liberals of western Canada have been most vociferous, our hon. friends would perhaps say, or, as we say, the most concerned, about the establishment of such a policy in the past years of Canada's history. Why? The answer of course is quite obvious, namely, that on the prairies we grow immense surpluses of foodstuffs and we must find a market for those surpluses. We could legislate here until doomsday, but unless we find markets at reasonable prices for the products of the west no legislation could be enacted that would make those people prosperous and contented. We must fundamentally shape our fiscal policy to encourage the finding of markets for those surpluses. In eastern Canada

The Budget-Mr. Graham
as I met them I found most hon. members who come from rural districts agreed with the classical argument, if you wish to call it that, for free trade; they were fundamentally in favour of free trade, but on account of the industrial centralization in this part of Canada they had to some extent a home market for the farm produce of .this part of Canada. That produce is of course that best suited to Ontario agriculture and their local market, namely, the raising of hogs and other live stock and the production of dairy products. Consequently, we never did get from eastern farm representatives the support to which I always felt the western people were entitled in their struggle to find markets for their products. But I want eastern members to note the tremendous change that has taken place during this war. Until the commencement of the war we in western Canada were concerned chiefly with the production of grain; to-day Alberta leads Ontario in the production of hogs, for example.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So does Manitoba.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. I mention that merely to illustrate the fact that western Canada has embarked upon a policy of producing immense quantities of the very things that were formerly left to Ontario and Quebec farmers to raise and market in the central provinces. This fact will have very great impact on I he agricultural situation in this country. I am hoping, therefore, that the farmers of Ontario and Quebec will realize quickly that they, like us, must find foreign markets for the surplus goods that we can so well produce. If we could find in the northwestern United States a market for the hogs, cattle and dairy products of western Canada we would not be in competition in the domestic market with the farmers of eastern Canada. But if you confine us by a protective tariff to attempting to find sale for our products in this small market, the products of Ontario and of the west will inevitably come into disastrous collision, and this will have a serious effect on agriculture in our whole Canadian economy.
Then let us look at the industrialization of Canada. For many years those who most favoured the protective policy were naturally those interested in the building up of manufactures in this country. We have all heard of the "infant industry"; although we do not hear that plan advanced so often now as formerly. But I say again to the industrialists of Canada, the war has shown that their possible production greatly exceeds the requirements of our domestic market. Their plants have been expanded; power facilities have been greatly increased, and the manufacturers of Canada will find themselves in
alignment with the farmers of eastern and western Canada in seeking foreign markets for their surplus products. Therefore I am hoping that at this historical moment the government will take full advantage of the opportunity presented to us now to put into effect some of the policies to which to a large extent the people of Canada have agreed but consider impossible of adoption for various local reasons. I know it takes at least two to make a bargain, even though we have the greatest desire in the world to adopt such a beneficial policy. But I must say that the advisability of adopting that policy would not depend on whether or not other countries did the same thing, though I know the attitude of the other country concerned would greatly influence the attitude of the average person toward such a policy. I think if the Minister of Finance were to study the history of that great country to the south, those 130,000,000 people who border us from the Atlantic to the Pacific, he would find that they, too, have learned many lessons as a result of this war and the last war. Perhaps never before, certainly never in my lifetime, has there been such an opportunity as is presented to this Liberal government to weld these countries together, to their mutual advantage.
To those who suggest that this would not be in complete consonance with our relationship to the mother country let me say in all sincerity that we must remember the position of Britain to-day and what will be her position after this terrible and prolonged war is over. Having in mind what will be Britain's financial position in the world after the war, I think we can best contribute to the British commonwealth of nations by making this Canada of ours as strong, as populous and as contented as we possibly can. Let us open our trade routes by sea, by rail and by air so that not only shall we profit by the exchange of goods that will follow, but we shall also help in the reconstruction of a world which will be sadly in need of the beneficent effects of such a wise policy. My purpose in making this speech to-day is solely in order to strengthen the hand of the government, for I have in mind that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has so capably acted as an intermediary between the United States and the mother country in the past. Let him complete that life work by taking the initiative in this matter as he took the initiative in uniting the war efforts of those countries, and in my opinion his name will be called blessed by the people of this country and particularly by the people of my own province.

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Souris)

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon his budget speech, and to a certain extent sympathize with him in the gigantic task of looking after the finances of this country in these very difficult times. In my opinion he is one of the most conscientious, hard-working members of the government. I should like also to offer my congratulations to my colleague the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) upon the very able manner in which he presented his criticisms of this budget. He certainly covered a wide field and did it very well.
The budget presented on March 2 calls for the raising of $5,500,000,000, which is certainly a sizable increase over the figure of $3,900,000,000 called for in the 1942 budget. The people of this country are prepared to pay, to work and to save, as they have been asked, provided there is not too much extravagance in the expenditure of public money. But when the government's director of economy is quoted in the press as was the case of March 4, as saying that evasion, subterfuge and outright trickery are being used to nullify the work of his office, then one wonders what is going on. Many people throughout this country are asking themselves questions when they see instances of money being wasted. In my opinion there is evidence of great waste in the expenditure of public money throughout this land, and I intend to deal with this matter at a later date. The rates of income tax in Canada are probably higher than those in any other country in the world; and with the exemptions lowered as they were a year ago, together with the increased demand for foodstuffs, many farmers have been brought into the income tax bracket for the first time. The minister stated that we are reaching the stage when we are producing all we can possibly produce from the resources and manpower at our disposal; and he went on to say that if we had no shortages, no vexatious restrictions, no farm labour problems such as have been debated in this house in recent weeks, then we could be certain that we were falling far short of an all-out war effort. I maintain that there has been an entire lack of coordination between the various departments of government in connection with our man-power problem. Up to the present it has been a case of inefficiency and muddling. If the Minister of Finance has any doubt as to that he might refer to the letter of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) under date of January 16, to the speech by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in

Saskatoon on January 21, and to the farm labour policy announced by the Minister of Labour on February 26. If these various statements are compared, it is enough to make one wonder whether there is any coordination at all in connection with this matter; and then when one considers the competition offered by industry and the armed forces with regard to man-power, it is no wonder that things are in such a muddle.
I have taken part in every budget debate in this house since 1940, and each time I have asked that the farmer's income should be ' averaged over a period of at least three years. I am pleased to note that the minister has gone at least some distance in that direction. Recently, however, a return was tabled in the house showing the number of farmers who have paid income tax each year since 1930, and it shows that in 1942 there were 1,488 farmers in that class. Many farmers are operating to-day under great difficulties, being very short of help. Where the wife or the teen-age boys and girls are doing the farm work-and in many instances doing it more efficiently than any hired help that might be obtained under the new farm labour set-up-they should be placed upon the farm payroll and their wages allowed as deductions in the income tax return. In the case of new machinery the farmer should be allowed to write it off on the same basis that is granted to industry during the war; that is, over a period of three years. The farmer is allowed to write off twenty per cent the first year and ten per cent thereafter in connection with the purchase of new equipment. The food supply is now second only to military operations in determining the outcome of this war, and it will take first place when it comes to saving the world from anarchy after the war is over. Yet the Minister of Finance or the government of the day has so far refused to allow parity prices for agricultural production in the same manner as is done for industry and organized labour.
Doctor Wallace, principal of Queen's university, and chairman of the subcommittee on natural resources of the dominion, committee on reconstruction, said last night, in the railway committee room of this building, when speaking under the auspices of the dominion command of the Canadian Legion, that the success of the nation would1 depend on the rural life of Canada; that next to equalized remuneration, which to me means parity, rural electrification probably meant more than anything else to the rural people of Canada. I am happy to know that a year ago the government of my native province of Manitoba produced a blueprint for rural farm electrification in this country.

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Souris)
But if we cannot establish during these critical times a parity price for essential goods and services, then the chances for post-war reconstruction and parity prices are, to say the least, not very bright. Great Britain is now producing approximately sixty per cent of her own foodstuffs. In Great Britain during 1939 there were some 12,000,000 acres under cultivation; to-day 18,000,000 acres are under cultivation. There were 53,000 tractors in use there before the commencement of the war. There are now 120,000 tractors, and other power machinery has increased accordingly.
In Canada this year new tractors supplied will number about 5,000. This is less than a third of the number sold last year. And most people will realize that the acreage under cultivation to-day in this country is practically three times that of Great Britain. I believe that the approximate number of tractors in Canada would be in the neighbourhood of 120,000, or the number in use in Great Britain. The latest figuers I have for Canada show that two years ago we had approximately 107,000 tractors.
In more normal times, some years ago, the farmers of western Canada spent about $50,000,000 annually upon farm implements. On account of depreciation, and as a result of lessened purchasing power for a number of years prior to the outbreak of war in 1939, it was estimated at that time by implement manufacturers that it would require approximately $200,000,000 to bring our farm implement equipment up to date.
The point I should like to make there is that, with our farm labour shortage, tractors, and especially combines, should be made available to as great an extent as is reasonably possible, in order to assist in solving our labour problems. I realize that the Minister of Agriculture who, I am glad to see, is in his seat, does not believe in the use of a tractor on a farm. That is his statement made in a recent debate.

As I said, that survey was conducted in 1932, when the cost of production was considerably less than it is to-day; and, of course, it was

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Souris)
based on eighteen bushels to the acre. Various other tests have been conducted throughout the country.
Other hon. members have quoted Professor Hope, and I should like now to refer to Professor Hope, who has charge of the department of farm management, university of Saskatchewan. He points out that the average cost, plus interest on debt, throughout Saskatchewan in recent years has been ninety-one cents a bushel, on the basis of an average yield of fourteen bushels to the acre, which is still considerably higher than the average yield throughout Canada. If one takes into account to-day the higher cost of living brought about by the recent budget it will advance those figures to considerably more than a dollar a bushel.
Professor Hope stated, as did Doctor Hopkins in his survey, that the most economic unit to operate in the prairie provinces was a two-section power farm with tractor combine and truck, and that that is the most efficient wheat-producing unit it is possible to set up at this time. But less than one per cent of the farms in the west are as efficiently operated as that unit. I cannot recollect the exact figures, but I know the average farm operated in the west is in the neighbourhood of a halfsection. As a matter of fact, I think it is a little less than a half-section. That is the basis upon which we have to consider the cost of production, as far as the average farmer of western Canada is concerned. And what applies to wheat production is equally true of feed grains.
I have also another article by J. E. Lattimer, professor of agricultural economics at Macdonald college. It deals with crops and wars. He has in this article a chart on which he gives some details as to the acreage of improved farm land per farm worker in the principal countries to date. I have before me a short article on distribution costs which was issued by the 20th century committee on distribution. It is pointed out here that approximately 59 cents of the consumer's dollar goes for the services of distribution and only 41 cents for the services of production.
As was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham), we in western Canada have made rapid changes toward diversified farming. I believe he stated that both Alberta and Manitoba now produce more hogs than Ontario. On February 4 when I spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I used a chart to show prices in Chicago and Winnipeg as of that date. In the case of hogs, both were quoted at $15.35 per 100 pounds, but that was dressed weight at Winnipeg and live weight at Chicago which meant approximately 25 per cent more for pork in the United States than was being received in Canada. The choice hog in the United States weighs from 190 to 330 pounds, as I then pointed out, while in Canada it runs from 190 to 230 pounds. You can put weight on a hog much cheaper per pound after 200 pounds is reached than you can up to that point.
All producers will realize that to produce the
800,000,000 pounds of pork with hogs of 165 pounds each, dressed weight, will require the raising of approximately five million hogs at 220 pounds live weight, or three and one-third million hogs at 330 pounds live weight. This means that the producer would need to carry only two-thirds the number of brood sows now required to produce the 800,000,000 pounds of pork asked for by the department. I should like to refer for a few moments to the production of flax for linseed oil. It is practically all grown in the prairie provinces-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The 1942 acreage was:
Manitoba	 227,000
Saskatchewan	 1,056,000
Alberta	 183,000
The total Canadian flax acreage for last year was 1,492,000.
The production of flax seed for oil purposes is now largely required for our war effort. During last summer and fall the farmers of western Canada were planning for a large increase of flax acreage this year. Many of them had bought seed at prices ranging from three dollars to five dollars a bushel. But, following the agricultural conference which was held in Ottawa on December 9, it was announced that the flax acreage for oil production should be increased by one million. The farmers went on making plans for increased production. About the middle of January the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) announced, rather suddenly, that as a result of a conference held in Washington at which he was present it was decided that no additional flax acreage should be put in during 1943, and he asked the farmers to go back to the original plan and produce from the same acreage as in 1942. A few days later there was a press release from the publicity and extension service of the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa, stating:
The United States department of agriculture, according to the latest survey, estimates that the country faces a shortage of close to a billion pounds of fats and oils for food and industrial purposes in 1943. To help overcome this shortage the government of Canada is asking for increased production of oil-producing plants such as flax, soy beans, sunflowers, etc. The objective for flax seed is an acreage increase of 68 per cent.
Following a meeting of the national barley and linseed flax committee at Winnipeg on March 1, Mr. L. H. Lehberg, technical adviser to the federal oils and fats administration, said that supplies of vegetable oils received from the United States had been below expectations and that United States crushers were in the market for Canadian flax in addition to overseas demand.
In addition to the domestic supplies, there were indications that upwards of ten million bushels of flax will be needed by the United States, and a like amount required for export overseas.
Among western farmers there is a feeling of confusion as to where they fit into this general

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Souris)
picture. This is well illustrated by the flax situation. Up to the present, with limited man-power and limited ability to secure the implements of production, of which I spoke this afternoon, they feel, as I stated, rather frustrated. The net marketable crop of flax last year was some 13,230,000 bushels. The total capacity for flax processing in this country was only 6,395,000 bushels, there being in operation nine flax processing plants, with one under construction at present. There are three of these plants in Montreal, two in Toronto, one in Baden, one in Winnipeg, one in St. Boniface, one in Medicine Hat, and one now under construction at Hamilton. It is rather surprising that this plant now being constructed at Hamilton should not have been built adjacent to the raw materials and abundance of cheap power which we have in the prairie provinces.
This afternoon, when the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was speaking, he pointed out that at present some eighty per cent of the capital in industry in Canada is invested within the two provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and that approximately eighty per cent of the industrial workers are located within these two provinces. As I have already indicated, this situation has been greatly aggravated during this war by the government of the day, by way of capital assistance to industry in Quebec and Ontario. I have placed on Hansard the sums of money which have been advanced, and which run into many hundreds of millions of dollars. Centralization apparently continues. A return of June 1 last shows that since the beginning of the war there had been constructed or were under construction in Ottawa eleven temporary buildings and one annex, at a total cost of $5,411,099.76. At that date, practically three years after the beginning of the war, only half of these buildings had been built. On February 26 there appeared in the press a statement that the government had approved a building programme under the National Housing Act and that in Ottawa and vicinity the sum of $1,000,000 was to be spent on the construction of houses, of which amount a quarter of a million was to be paid by the government.
Yesterday the Ottawa Journal published an editorial article entitled " More 'temporary' buildings," from which I quote the following:
The government announces that an office building for the staff of prices board is to be built on Sussex street, at a cost of about $450,000. Prices board staff now is scattered about several rented premises. The government is to spend also $312,000 for a building for the women's division of the R.C.A.F., and $54,205 for a men's canteen. All of these are to be "temporary" structures.

In the grand total of war expenditures $800,000 does not rank as a major item, and yet we think the people-who pay the bills- would like more assurance than appears on the surface that these buildings are an imperative necessity. That is especially the case as they are still in the plans stage, and if we may judge by the progress of work on the women's hostel the buildings would not be ready for use before next Christmas. The point is, do we really need these costly and elaborate "temporary" buildings when the war will he well within its fifth year?
Further on it says:
A few days ago Mr. Ilsley announced that indefinite extension of government-financed housing would he impossible, because of scarcity of labour and materials, and to relieve the housing shortage, he said, the government would depend upon "private enterprise, rent control and decentralization". Some progress in decentralization already had been made, he added, pointing out that more than a dozen branches of prices board had been moved to Toronto and Montreal; that munitions and supply had established oil control in Toronto, transport control in Montreal.
Obviously, the extent to which the government proposes to pursue this policy of decentralization must he a factor in the case for these new buildings. And at this stage of the war the demand for new office space by any department or agency of the government, or any uniformed service, needs to be viewed with healthy scepticism and an inquiring mind.
As most people know, we have at the head of the wartime prices and trade board Mr. Donald Gordon, a banker, who has not any experience whatever in production, distribution or merchandising within this country. The price of fuel wood in parts of Canada has been increased, by a stroke of the pen, from $9 to $13 a cord. You pay an extra five cents for a cup of tea or coffee for your meal. Yet the agriculturists of Canada are asked to produce foodstuffs for much less remuneration than the agriculturists of any other of the warring nations receive at this particular time. If we are to enforce the principle of price ceilings the price must be on a basis of parity prices for essential goods and services. This is something which to date the government of the day has not recognized. As I have pointed out before, the agriculturists represent thirty-three per cent of our entire population. They received fifteen per cent of the national income in the past year, 1942, and during the years from 1915 to 1919 they received thirty per cent of the national income. Certain large business concerns are now consolidating their position in this country under the present scheme of things.
May I add with respect to the wartime prices and trade board that on June 29 of last year I placed on the order paper a question asking for detailed information as to the

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
board's staff. That question remained unanswered on the order paper until prorogation on January 27 of this year.. I again placed it on the order paper on January 29 of this session, and it was passed as an order for a return on February 8, but to this day the return has not been brought down. A lot of pertinent information should be brought down in that return. I do not want to weary the house by giving the details of this question because it is lengthy, but I would point out, as was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for New Westminster, that there is great discontent throughout this country because of the operations of the price control administration under Mr. Donald Gordon, and the only reason why people are not saying more about it is their patriotism in this time of war. I am satisfied, however, that there must be a basis of parity prices for goods and services which are essential to the war effort; otherwise the board cannot continue to operate.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding to speak on that aspect of the budget which I wish particularly to discuss, I should like to make two or three observations of a general nature. I believe that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in his recent remarks with respect to financial policy, which of course have their counterpart in economic policy, has served to prove more effectively than he could have done so deliberately the truth of many things which we in this group have been asserting over a period of time.
We believe that time will be the best test of right. We also believe that over a certain period of time certain prejudices which have existed will gradually disappear. We feel, as I said before, that the minister could not have been more successful in attesting the authenticity of many of these things that we have declared to be facts if he had deliberately set out to do so.
A few days ago a member of this house, sitting to the left, Mr. Speaker, expressed the fear that through the enormous financial expansion and through the enormous allocations of real wealth taking place in this country there was a danger we might go bankrupt. In reply to that expression of fear the minister made some significant declarations, and it is about those declarations that I should like to make one or two observations.
The Minister of Finance said that to speak of bankrupting this country simply because of the expenditure of billions of dollars or because of the consumption through war or otherwise of vast quantities of our production was simply to bring forward a bogey. He
asserted that an individual or a group of individuals might go bankrupt in that way, and that even a nation might go bankrupt in that way as far as the supply of foreign exchange was concerned. But he said that as far as the nation itself is concerned it is fantastic to assume that we might become bankrupt in the sense that we shall run out of money. In fact, he said, the danger in war time is just the opposite. If we are going to become bankrupt because of these actions of ours, is it not a strange thing, he asked, that at the same time we are doubling the national income, wiping out unemployment, learning scores of new skills, and that we have expanded and diversified our productive equipment, enabled millions of our people to secure a nest-egg for the future, and developed a sense of productive achievement hitherto unknown in this country? He stated that no country goes bankrupt in that way; no country goes bankrupt through expanding its productive capacity. That, Mr. Speaker, was a significant statement. I know that it has been responsible for a number of very strange expressions which have emanated from certain members sitting on the government side of the house.
In the years of the depression members of this group advocated the stimulation of production through government grants. The Minister of Finance of that day-not the present minister, but he seemed to think along the same lines-threw his hands up in the air and screamed blue ruin. Yet to-day we find the Minister of Finance of the present government asserting that if we spend more money to expand the productive capacity of our country it is utterly impossible for this country as a consequence to go bankrupt. That should make us think. At this time we have about 600,000 of our men and women in uniform. They are not engaged in a productive capacity. We have taken up the slack as far as unemployment is concerned; yet we find that we are producing more than twice as much as we ever produced before. That is enough to make anyone stop and think. As we reflect upon post-war conditions we shall also bear in mind the statements made by the Minister of Finance to the effect that there is no danger of bankrupting your country by putting further quantities of money into circulation and vastly expanding the productive capacity of your country.
I wish to devote my time this evening mainly to the one aspect of war finance. Probably I should clarify my statement by saying that I intend to deal specifically with the war savings aspect of our war finance pro-
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

gramme. I do so because I am afraid that many hon. members are not aware of the situation that has developed in this country with respect to war finance.
The minister stated the other day that the expenditures during 1942-I assume that means until March 31 of this year-will amount to $4,470 million. He stated further, either directly or by implication, that that volume of money in circulation, or at least a large part of that money which will be put into circulation, may, on account of the lesser amount of consumer goods available, create a dangerous condition of inflation. And because of that danger he will have to institute upon a larger scale his war savings campaign in order to tap from the finances in circulation in the country that portion which is likely to cause a condition of inflation.
At this point I should like to make one thing clear. There are many hon. members in this house and people in this country who actually believe that the only purpose of a bond campaign is to secure money with which to purchase ships and shells and guns and tanks. I have stated that one of the major purposes of a bond selling campaign is to drain off the excess purchasing power, and I have been roundly criticized for that statement. In order that my position in that regard may be made quite clear I should like to quote three or four statements which I have before me. First, I have a statement of the financial secretary to the British treasury, speaking in the British House of Commons on April 8, 1941. He said:
What you have to emphasize is not so much the money that you are going to get in but the fact that what you are after is reducing consumption.
Then we have the Royal bank monthly letter of August, 1941, saying:
It is, therefore, vitally important that taxation and borrowing should be considered not merely as devices to raise money but rather as measures to prevent money from being spent for non-essential purposes.
Professor Plumptre is reported in the Financial Post of October 5, 1940, as saying:
It must be remembered primarily and seemingly paradoxically, that the government object is not to get money, but merely to reduce the public's spending. . . . The government can always "get money" because it may as an alternative to borrowing or even to taxation, create the required funds.
Then we have P. M. Richards, financial editor of Saturday Night, saying on March 28, 1942:
The hard truth is that the government didn't itself want our money as much as it wanted to deprive us of it.

Then we have the Minister of Finance himself, speaking in the House of Commons on November 21, 1949, saying:
That the task of finance is not only to provide the funds which are used to pay for the war services but more fundamentally is, by taxing and borrowing, to restrict the civilian demand for economic resources.
My purpose in quoting as I have is to be able to deal with the situation which has developed with respect to the war savings campaign. I shall deal with that a little later. I say the purpose of the bond, war savings certificates and stamp sales is primarily to drain off the surplus purchasing power and thus lessen the danger of an inflationary condition developing.
I stated that I should like to give some information with respect to the trend in connection with bond sales. In the second victory loan, of about a year ago, the government secured about $843 million from the Canadian people. If we forget for the moment the conversions that took place during that time, that sum exceeded the objective by about forty per cent.
Then we come to the third victory loan of last fall which secured, I believe, about $991,500,000 which, if considered less conversions, was approximately thirty-two per cent more than the stated objective. I would point out that not all the money so acquired came from savings; a large part of it came as a consequence of payroll deductions and other payments out of current income. Between February, 1942, and November, 1942, namely, between the second and third victory loans, there was a total of 339,000 conversions. Those conversions were mainly of $50 and $100 bonds. In October, 1942, alone the conversions numbered 78,000, or approximately 3,000 per working day. That is startling. Of the 339,000 conversions to which I have already referred, 268,000 represented bonds of $50 denomination, and 71,000 those of $100 denomination.
I have some figures which are very interesting. They are month by month figures from March to November of 1942, as follows:
