In the second victory loan I believe we had approximately 1,120,000 subscriptions for $50 bonds and approximately 746,000 subscriptions for S100 bonds. The dollar value of the conversions was not high, but the important thing to bear in mind is this. The minister has stated from time to time that through his bond selling campaigns he has endeavoured to spread the purchases over as broad a base as possible, thus depriving a greater number of those in the moderate income brackets of a part of their purchasing power, because, after all, they comprise the largest single group of all those in receipt of salaries. I believe the number of subscribers to the second victory loan totaled
1,681,000,	while the number who subscribed to the third victory loan was slightly in excess of 2,000,000. Therefore, if the conversion of $50 and $100 bonds is going on now as rapidly as it did prior to November, 1942, I am of opinion that by the middle of next summer we shall have over 400,000 conversions.
I would ask that these figures be kept in mind, because I am leading up to something *which I believe to be of extreme importance. In the second victory loan I understand that something like 800,000 workers participated in the payroll deduction plan, subscribing approximately $65,000,000. In the third victory loan there were about 1,200,000 who subscribed approximately $90,000,000 under the same plan. These were mainly bonds in the $50 and $100 denominations, and I would say it is in those brackets that wTe face the greatest number of conversions. Those conversions were extremely heavy last September, and I believe the reason was that bonds purchased, during the second victory loan matured, if that is a proper word to use, about that time. This leads me to believe that a very large number of those who purchased bonds during the second victory loan campaign cashed them in just as soon as the law permitted them to do so. I think the same applies also to the sales of war savings certificates. I understand that of the $6,000,000 worth of certificates sold between the second and third victory loans, approximately $2,000,000 were handed in for redemption.
This is extremely important, I believe, in the light of what I have to say in a moment or two. It seems to me the results of such a scheme are extremely obvious. On the surface it would appear that the very fine machinery set up by the minister in order to handle the savings aspect of his finance policy is breaking down much more rapidly than many people anticipated; I was going to say more rapidly than the minister expected, but I do not think 72537-75
that would be fair because I believe he appreciates the situation that is developing. Let me give what I think are the reasons for so many conversions in the $50 and $100 brackets. The first is the nature of the campaigns that have been carried on; I believe that is responsible to a certain extent. You cannot withhold from the people the fact that the main reason for pushing the sale of bonds, war savings certificates and stamps is to reduce the public demand for consumer goods. They find it out sooner or later. I know that many persons sacrificed beyond their capacity because they were assured that the only way in which we could produce ships, shells, guns and tanks was for them to deprive themselves in order to purchase war savings stamps, certificates and bonds. As a result, the moment the time arrived when they could legally convert those bonds into cash, they did so.
I should like to develop that point just a little further. If one of the principal reasons-and I dare even go so far as to say the major reason-behind the bond sale campaign of the government is to reduce the public demand for consumer goods, in my opinion it is a serious thing to say in theatres, at public meetings and in various other ways that a certain boy on a certain ship will not have a gun if you do not deprive yourself of some necessity in order to buy a bond. The people find out the real reason sooner or later. For instance, all they had to do was to pick up Maclean's magazine for last October 13 and read the article in which the minister definitely asserted, in reply to a question, that one major purpose behind the campaign was to reduce the public demand for consumer goods. His salesmen go to old age pensioners, for example, and in some instances they have actually made them feel that if they did not subscribe they were subversive. I am not blaming the minister for that; I am blaming some of the salesmen who apparently have not been properly advised with respect to these points. No one is capable of putting up a good argument to the effect that an old age pensioner receiving anywhere from $10 to $25 a month has any surplus purchasing power which will endanger the national economy. The same can be said of a widowed mother, a man in receipt of war veterans' allowance, or even a man in receipt of a veteran's pension. They resent it when somebody comes along and puts pressure on them, compelling them to make sacrifices out of all proportion to what

The Budget-Mr. Shaw

Canadians generally are sacrificing. Consequently the moment they can do so many convert their bonds into cash.
I should like to say a word about payroll deductions. In doing so, I wish to talk about the civil service. All across this country we have thousands upon thousands of people in receipt of incomes far below those to which they are entitled in order to meet the increased costs of living. The government has not set a very good example in this regard, because government offices in Ottawa and across the country are filled with young girls and young men whose incomes are certainly not adequate to meet the costs of living with which they are confronted.
The war savings committee goes to those young girls and young men and makes their contributions almost a condition of employment. No wonder the minute they have an opportunity of converting their purchases into cash, they do so! I made a rather strong statement when I said that even in the civil service contributions are practically made a condition of employment.
In that connection let me quote from something which came to my hand. It is a pamphlet headed "The federal civil service organization", and makes reference to the third victory loan campaign. I would ask hon. members to bear in mind that we are always using the word "voluntary" and emphasizing that all these contributions are voluntary. The pamphlet reads, in part, as follows:
The federal civil service forms part of payroll savings section of the national war finance committee's organization for the purposes of the third victory loan.
The appeal to you-
And I ask hon. members to mark the word "appeal".
-as a Canadian is to share in the subscribing of $750,000,000 for the national war effort. The demand of you-
Note those words:
-as a civil servant is to organize and support the loan in order that the flag may fly high in your locality.
And listen to the next paragraph:
The governor in council has directed that every civil servant invited to serve on a committee organized by or for the national war finance committee shall accept the task as an act of duty.	_
Every civil service victory loan group officially organized for the purposes of the victory loan is subject to such direction and supervision as the national war finance committee, or its provincial or local divisions and units, may deem necessary.
I shall not go beyond that point, but I believe I have read enough to indicate that no government employee, regardless of

whether she or he is receiving S55, $60 or $70 a month dared refuse to subscribe. And I know that some of these young employees who have been drawn from the west to work in Ottawa-because you will not give us industry or war departments to any extent out in the west-try to save their nickels and dimes so that they may go home for two weeks during the summer. No wonder thousands of them have quit! No wonder that when I called for a return showing how many had quit I was told that the government did not have the information!
Those are some of the reasons. Let me emphasize the fact that while these young employees are underpaid, while they are having this pressure put upon them to purchase, it is no wonder that after the great machine is paid to collect they turn around and convert their bonds.
Then, there is another reason, which has to do with our boys and girls in uniform. I contend that when we stop to consider what they are being paid-and I am not complaining about it for the moment, although I certainly think it is inadequate-we must remember that they are prepared to make the supreme sacrifice. Yet I should like to tell the house what happened in connection with this same war savings campaign in the military camps. I know of eight hundred soldiers right in this province who were taking a special course. In the third victory loan campaign they had placed upon their shoulders a quota of $16,000, which meant $20 per soldier. Any soldier who did not subscribe to the extent of $20 was paraded before his commanding officer, and when that happened he had to give good reasons for not having subscribed. I dare say that rather than be paraded before his commanding officer the average man would sacrifice, or would have his family make sacrifices, in order to keep up his head among the other men in his unit. But the minute it became legal or possible to convert those bonds into cash, naturally they would do so.
Then, there is another reason. I wish to refer to the contents of a letter which came to my attention only two days ago. The Minister of Finance is not in his seat at the moment, but I should like to have someone tell him about this, so that he can check it. This letter from my constituency states-and I shall not quote the man's exact words- that the collector for the International Harvester Company in that part of our province stated he had been instructed by his company to secure $3,000,000 in bonds on past due accounts, as well as on new accounts. If that is true-and I am sure the minister would get the significance of it-it certainly should be

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
checked. I am told in the same letter that a certain bond salesman in that town purchased all the bonds he could possibly buy with the spare cash he had on hand, then went out and flourished those bonds under the noses of prospective subscribers, to show them what a patriotic man he was. Very shortly after the campaign closed he went to the bank and had his bonds converted into cash, following which he installed an expensive electric lighting plant in his farm buildings.
Those are practices which are not good. When the people in that community find out that such things took place they will naturally endeavour to dispose of their bonds as quickly as possible. I say that if the minister does not want this great war savings campaign machine to bog down he had better do something about repairing some of the broken parts in it, and apply a little oil; because, as sure as can be, if the rate of conversion continues it will be only a short time until our conversions are almost equal to our purchases, and this very danger about which he has been warning us will be upon us, and upon us before he realizes it.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of features of this year's budget concerning which our people will exercise their right to grumble; but in the main I am satisfied the people will accept the budget, because of their willingness to put everything they have into their endeavour to achieve victory, in the hope and determination that after the war has been won we shall win a people's peace here at home. Perhaps more important than any grumbling on the part of our people, one should state that this is a budget which they will not forget. I am referring not to its severity, but rather to the way in which it turns the searchlight on the importance of the common man. In particular this budget points out that it is impossible to collect in taxes the amount of money that is necessary to wage the war without dipping very heavily into the pockets of those with meagre incomes. The budget also points out that it is impossible to borrow sufficient money to meet the requirements of the war without calling upon the common people, the great mass of workers and farmers, to give of their savings. The budget also points out that in the matter of restricting the demands for domestic goods, again the appeal must be made to the common people. We cannot restrict that demand sufficiently by asking the well-to-do to go without their luxuries; the only way it can be done is 72537-75J
by getting the common people to curtail their purchases of some of the actual necessities of life.
We in this group, and many throughout the country, are not satisfied that this budget goes as far as it should in placing the proper share of the burden upon those in the upper brackets, but we admit that the budget draws attention to the fact that even though heavier burdens are placed on those in the upper brackets, it is still necessary to call upon the great mass of the common people, the workers and the farmers, if we are to find the wherewithal to wage this conflict. In other words, this budget turns the searchlight on the importance of the common people. It is the common people who must fight the war; it is the common people who must produce the munitions of war and the food; and it is the common people who must provide the finances, and refrain from demanding domestic goods so that we can divert the portion that is necessary to war materials. I urge, as I have already stated, that the common man be not forgotten. If he is so important to-day, he will be important to-morrow.
In my view there would be less complaining about the budget if there were a few gestures on the other side to the importance of the common man. In addition to the importance given him through asking him to fight the war, to produce the goods and to provide the finance, his needs should be recognized! to a much greater extent than is the case-as far as this budget is concerned. I wish to-speak specifically about two or three groups-of our citizens for whom it seems to me thia is the time that consideration should be given. I shall refer first to the old age and blind pensioners.
In 1939-40 the total expenditures of this government were 8080,794,000. The budget for this year calls for $5,500,000,000. In other words, this year's budget is $4,819,206,000 greater than the expenditures of 1939-40. Back in 1939 old age pensions were being debated in this house. I find on page 1746 of Hansard of that year that the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, dealt with this question by pointing out that in order to lower the age at which old age pensions would be paid to sixty-five years-that was the matter being discussed at that particular moment-would cost the dominion alone the sum of $18,859,000. That amount simply could not be found, and therefore no change was made in the Old Age Pensions Act.
I go back to the figures I gave a moment ago. In 1939 it was impossible to find
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

$18,859,000, but the expenditures to be made this year will exceed the total expenditures of 1939-40 by 255 times the increase which could not be found in 1939.
I hold in my hand a copy of a letter written by the attorney general of Manitoba to the president of the old age pensioners society in that province under date of June 18, 1942. In this letter Mr. McLenaghan quotes part of a letter which he had received from the Minister of Finance of this government. The Minister of Finance, referring to the total cost of old age and blind pensions for 1941-42 had this to say:
If the maximum pension had been $300 a year the total cost of pensions would have been increased by approximately $9,870,600.
The writer of the letter then goes on to set out the portion of that amount which the provinces would have been required to contribute, but that portion is included in this total sum of less than ten million dollars. Ten million dollars sounds like a lot of money, but it represents only an additional one-fifth of one cent for every dollar that we shall spend this year. The amount is so small, such a drop in the 'bucket, that it seems to me deplorable, if not disgraceful, that no provision for an increase in the amount to be paid for old age and blind pensioners is being made in this year's budget.
It is rather sad to note that according to the estimates the amount to be voted for old age pensions this year is $126,000 less than was voted last year. I take it there are only two explanations for this. Either the amounts are being cut down by means of the various regulations, or the old people are dying off. One cannot be surprised at that when he thinks of their trying to exist on $20 a month. On the other hand, I note that the estimates provide for an increase of nearly $3,000 in the amount required for pensions to retired judges.
I think the views of the people generally, outside the house, and of the majority of those inside the house, although these views do not often find expression from the government benches, are very well put in the report of a sermon delivered recently by Reverend Father Wood of St. Mary's Cathedral, Winnipeg. I should like to quote from a report in the Winnipeg Tribune of January 26, as follows:
The way we are treating our old pioneers by granting them the magnificent sum of $20 a month each is a disgrace to any civilized country, Rev. F. R. Wood said at St. Mary's cathedral Sunday.
"You know the situation regarding old_ age and blind pensions," he said. "The sum is so small as barely to exclude starvation, especially
.
when the recipient is deprived of almost everything he possesses before even this miserable pittance is granted.
"If two people succeed in building a home and then in their old age lose their income, the authorities seize this last thing and insist on rendering them destitute before granting them $20 a month."
"We are not actually guilty of killing our old people, but we are approaching as close to that state as we dare go without being brought into the courts."
I hope that the day will come when the attitude in this house toward old age pensions, instead of making possible statements such as this I have read from Father Wood, will be that which has been brought to the attention of this house before from a sister dominion. I quote from what was said in the parliament of New Zealand on September 1, 1936:
All social legislation, and especially that providing for pensions, is a recognition by the community of the fact that the recipients of the pension have in a very large measure been responsible for the development of the country and the vast accumulations within it. One of the points to be recognized is that such allowances made by the younger generation to their forebears are by no means a charity but in reality a recognition and a return to them of what they themselves have put into the nation.
A few days ago I asked some questions in the house concerning this matter, whether or not this government had given any hope to the various provinces that some adjustment in the amount of the old age pension might be made; and among the answers that I received, I find that I was referred to a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), I believe it was in 1941. On looking into that statement I discovered that one of the points which the minister laid down on that occasion was either his belief or the belief of his party that the only way in which we could hope for an increase in the amount of the old age pension was to put it on a contributory basis. I think the answer to that point is very clearly put in the words I have quoted from the New Zealand Hansard, to the effect that our old people have already contributed to the wealth and well-being of the country and, because of the contribution which they have made, if for no other reason, they are entitled to decency and dignity in their old age-which is not possible on the $20 a month we are giving them at the present time.
Not only are there our old people, but there are other groups in the community for whom, it seems to me, this budget should have made better provision. A number of us in the last day or two have had the privilege of meeting with a group of ladies who are in the city at the present time, representing the non-pensioned widows of veterans of

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
the last war. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) stated this afternoon that the country would receive well the item of $400,000 which is in the estimates to make some provision for these people. He is perfectly right; this country will receive well the fact that something is being done: but it seems to me that the country will not rest at all easy when it realizes that that provision boils down to $20, or in special cases to $25 as a maximum, a month for these women when they are in necessitous circumstances and when they meet certain other regulations which will be laid down from time to time. It seems to me that this is a disgrace to the memory of the men who gave their lives in, or as a result of, the last war; that it is a disgrace, in the light of the things that are being said about what this war is being fought for, if this is the best we can do for these women. I sincerely hope that hon. members by an overwhelming majority will have so much to say on this matter that a change of policy will be made by the government before this session is over, either that the amount to be granted to these people will be raised, or that the possibility of any means test will be eliminated, or both of these, with other provisions as well. I suggest that if a few gestures of this nature could have been provided for in the budget, it would have eliminated any grumbling about it on the part of our people, and it would have done the thing I suggested1 earlier; it would have made our people, the workers and the farmers, feel that not only were they important when it comes to fighting the war and providing the goods and paying for it, but their needs also are important, and they have the right to participate in the wealth and well-being of this country. I hope that before this session is over, despite the fact that the policy has been announced and the estimates have 'been laid on the table, a revision will be made, recognizing on that side of things the importance of the common people of this dominion.
I turn now to another matter. A very large section of these important common people, these people who fight the war and produce the supplies and pay for it, are working men and women. The attitude of this government toward labour is a matter of great importance to them. Thus far that attitude does not give them a great deal of hope for a better day. I want to refer to what I have in my hand as an example. This document is a copy of a return tabled in the Manitoba legislature on February 22. It sets out certain facts which are public property:	first of all, that in
November, 1941, certain underpayments of
wages on dominion government contracts within the province of Manitoba were discovered. On looking into this matter, I find that the wages paid were in accordance with what this government requires as a minimum but they were underpayments as far as legislation in the province of Manitoba is concerned. The then minister of labour of Manitoba, according to a press report of his remarks in the legislature, said quite definitely that for a period of a great many months his department was given to understand that the dominion government would require the enforcement of Manitoba fair wage legislation on dominion government contracts within the province, even though the wages required there might be higher than those required by the regulations of this government. This document which I have in my hand says further that in March, 1942, a report on these underpayments was made to the Department of Labour of this government. The department of labour of Manitoba asked the permission of the Department of Labour here to collect these alleged underpayments. The federal Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) agreed to this proposal on April 17, 1942. I suggest that the statement in this connection in this return supports the contention made by the former minister of labour of Manitoba, that for a time at least he had the approval of this government for the enforcement in Manitoba of the province's fair wage legislation with respect to dominion government contracts in -that province. But in the course of time- again I am reading from the return which I have in my hand-one of the companies there protested and wrote to Ottawa, referring the matter to the chief of wages branch of the national war labour board; and on October 7, 1942, the chief of that branch wrote to the-then minister of labour of Manitoba advising: him that the matter had been referred to the federal Department of Justice. Matters went on until January 14 of this year when the federal Minister of Labour reported to the regional war labour board of the province of Manitoba the decision of the Department of Justice at Ottawa. I shall read the important clause, clause (c):
The works in question are not subject to the fair wages act, 1916, of Manitoba.
Yesterday when I had before the house a motion asking for the tabling of certain documents passing between this government and the provincial governments, respecting the matter of old age pensions, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made the reservation that the documents should not be brought
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

down to the house until the provincial governments had been consulted. I quote his remarks from page 1129 of Hansard:
The provinces have their own jurisdiction and they are partners in the work of government of the dominion.
In another passage he says that the provinces are sensitive about the federal government stepping in. But when it is a case of provincial wage legislation calling for slightly higher wages than the dominion legislation calls for, this government does not hesitate to step in and, in effect, nullify that higher wage legislation of the province of Manitoba.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do I understand that the correspondence which my hon. friend has read is the subject of a return brought down to this house?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The correspondence I have read is from a return tabled in the Manitoba legislature. When I asked questions concerning this matter in the house a few days ago, the Minister of Labour stated that a commissioner had been appointed to make an investigation. But, Mr. Speaker, this is not a matter for investigation; it is a matter of policy. The companies concerned do not dispute the question of the wages which were paid to their employees or the hours their employees worked, but they dispute the right of the Manitoba government to insist on the payment of Manitoba wages on dominion government work.
What has happened is that there has been a reversal of policy on the part of this government. The policy enunciated by the Minister of Labour on April 17, 1942, was that this government agreed to the right of the Manitoba government to enforce its own wage legislation, but on January 14, 1943, we find that this government changed its policy. I know there is a reference to a ruling from the Department of Justice, and in the minds of some people there is something very sacrosanct about a ruling of the Department of Justice. But after all that is not a ruling of the courts. It is simply a ruling of another department of the government. Undoubtedly there has been a change of policy on the part of the government, a willingness to interfere and actually to nullify the wage legislation that exists in Manitoba. I repeat, that is not a matter for investigation; it is a matter of policy.
This attitude on the part of the Department of Labour of this government does not alleviate the grumbling of our people about the budget. On the other hand I feel that if we 
had a labour policy moving in a progressive direction we would have less complaining about the severity of the budget.
There are one or two other related matters which were given publicity in the press of Winnipeg, following an address in the provincial legislature of Manitoba by the former minister of labour there. About an hour ago some of us had the privilege of sitting down to a delightful dinner as the guests of one of the hon. members from Winnipeg, and because of the nature of the food served we had some very good fish stories. This is a fish story that is not quite so enjoyable.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How were the fish?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The fish were lovely. I quote from the press report:
In December, 1941, a complaint was received that a fish company supplying fish on a war contract, was not paying the minimum wage.
That is the Manitoba minimum wage.
An inspector investigated. Attached to the contract was a wage schedule. On inquiry it was found the company owed $67 and gave a cheque for it.
Mr. Farmer told the house his department was asked to send it to Ottawa from where it would be disbursed to the persons entitled to it. Some time after the men asked when they could expect their cheques. In March, 1942-
Note, that was in March, 1942, and yet a month later, on April 17, 1942, the Department of Labour here was still giving authority to the Manitoba department to enforce these wages. I continue the quotation:
In March, 1942, he discovered that the cheque he had collected had been returned to the fish company with the explanation that the contract did not come within what were interpreted as war contracts.
On another occasion, training schools were set up in certain clothing factories and other industries under dominion regulations with respect to the war emergency training programme. As one inducement to get trainees the dominion published a schedule promising wages of 35 cents an hour to those who took the course. During the training period the apprentices were paid by the dominion.
Some employers who took on the trainees, after they had finished the course, employed them at the minimum wage, 25 cents an hour. When attempts were made to collect the 35 cents promised, word came from Ottawa that the whole thing had been a mistake.
There you had on the part of the province of Manitoba a readiness to enforce, to go out diligently to enforce a wage scale slightly better than the wage scale of this government. But this government, which, as I suggested from the Prime Minister's remarks yesterday, at times declares that it does not want to interfere in provincial matters, did not hesitate to step in and nullify the provincial wage

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
legislation. Then they wonder why there are complaints about the labour policy of this government.
Closely related, turning for a moment to the agricultural community, is the concern- and some of us are beginning to get quite a bit of correspondence about it-as to whether cooperative organizations will have to pay taxes on the money which they save by their cooperative endeavours. There are very disquieting rumours. If this should be the case; if there is to be a policy that will ruin the cooperative movement in this country, as well as having an anti-labour policy, I suggest that the people are going to wonder whether there is anything at all to the professions that are frequently made around here about this being a war for a better world when victory is won. If some of the aims of our social legislation which I have suggested, an increase in the old age pension, an increase in the amount set aside for widows of veterans of the last war, and an increase in wages along the lines I have just suggested were granted, I realize that we would be moving slightly in the direction of a better order, slightly in the direction of a greater share by the Canadian people in the wealth they produce. There may be some who do not like that idea. But supposedly that is what this war is all about, and I suggest that if the people of this country are as important as they are when it comes to fighting the war, producing the goods required, and paying for the war, they are important in these other respects as well.
There is another matter which has been of deep concern to the people of Winnipeg. It is perhaps only a small matter taken by itself, but if it is a sample it creates misgivings. Not long ago the government purchased for war needs, I believe by the Department of National Defence for Naval Services, a property in Winnipeg formerly known as the Winnipeg Winter club. I made inquiry both in Winnipeg and here concerning this purchase, and I hold in my hand a copy of sessional paper No. 193. I asked several questions, two being particularly relevant. I endeavoured to ascertain the assessed value of the property and to discover what had been paid for it. According to the sessional paper the assessed value of land and buildings was $129,365. In that connection may I say I have secured similar information from the assessment commissioner of Winnipeg and it tallies with this figure, but I make this comment, that the figures I received from Winnipeg give the amount on which the taxes were paid as $94,090. The assessment commissioner, however, advises me what percentage of the market
value these figures represented, and when you adjust that figure, the $129,365 represents the market value as computed from the assessed valuation. But the price paid for the land, building and equipment was $256,000. I wish to make it perfectly clear that the assessed value did not include the equipment while the purchase price did, but there is a spread there of over $126,000, which is a lot of money for the equipment which could have been in that property.
I find as an explanation of this purchase that the price was arrived at after consultation between a member of the Montreal real estate board - not the board - and members - not the board itself-of the Winnipeg real estate board, and the real estate adviser of the Department of National Defence. And then note this sentence. I suppose it is a defence; I need not comment on it:
A condition of the sale was that the Winnipeg Winter club would invest the total net proceeds in victory bonds-
"the total net proceeds", I wonder what that "net" means.

and would undertake to retain and not to dispose of by sale at least fifty per cent of the said bonds for the duration of the war.
That sort of thing puzzles people who are asked to pay in the way our people are asked to pay, when $256,000 is paid for a piece of property the market value of which, as adjusted from the assessed value, was only $129,365.
Another matter which causes deep concern to our people is the amount of unnecessary advertising which is being circulated in our newspapers and put upon billboards across the country. I hold in my hand a full page advertisement; it does not matter whose it is because a great many firms are doing it. It offers nothing for sale; but apparently the money has to be spent in some way; the newspapers have to be kept going, or perhaps what is more to the point private industry has to be kept in the field until the war is over. Some may say, What is wrong with that? But I insist that that is not what the common people are fighting for, for the maintenance by private industry of a grip on our economy. Our people are concerned about a new economy in which they will have the opportunity, free from the restrictions of private profit, to produce an abundance of wealth and forthwith to share in that wealth.
In closing, let me say that some of us regret very much that into this budget debate there has come the old issue of tariffs and free trade. It has been introduced on the one hand by the Minister of Finance and on the other hand by the first speaker for the official opposition.
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

It causes some of us misgivings to feel that possibly when this war is over, our boys will come home to be handed once again the age-old political battle between these two groups. The point was very well put in a recent broadcast over the C.B.C. in which Mr. J. W. Dafoe, editor of the Winnipeg Free Press, took part in which he made a statement something like this-I am paraphrasing it, but I think I have the sense of what he said: The trouble with the planners-and when the Winnipeg Free Press talks about "planners" it is usually talking about the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation-is that they aim at sharing what we have within our country on a subsistence basis. The trouble with the planners is that they do not realize or are not prepared to try to take advantage of the values to be had from foreign trade.
I say that that last charge is not correct; we are deeply concerned about the values to be had by foreign trade; but what we wish to point out to those who think like Mr. Dafoe, is that you can have a trade policy that will result in gains for Canada as a whole, but unless within the country you have some sort of planned economy, the common people will not profit from those gains from foreign trade. In other words, we believe that what is needed is a wise policy as far as foreign trade is concerned so that we shall reap the advantages to be had by an economic division of labour among the various quarters of the earth, and in addition an internal policy on the basis of a planned economy so that our people will share in the benefits to be gained from that foreign trade, as well as from our own production.
We in this group are sometimes accused of not being interested in the matter of trade. We are deeply interested. But we deplore the fact that those who are concerned primarily with tariff matters do not realize the importance of the other side of the picture, namely, the ways and means within our country whereby we can share the wealth we produce or gain by a wise trade policy.
I believe that the subamendment moved by this group expresses very well the views of the people of this country, particularly the workers and the farmers, with respect to the budget: first of all that there should be the nationalization of our banking system. We are able to follow the arguments of the Minister of Finance concerning the necessity of borrowing from the chartered banks, under the set-up that now exists. But we see no reason why this government, since it has supreme control over banking and monetary policy, should not nationalize the banks and 
then see to it that the amount of money we have to borrow to supplement savings and taxation is borrowed from our own banking system without mortgaging the future of this country in terms of heavy interest payments.
Second, our subamendment proposes-and I am sure it represents very clearly the views of our people-that there should have been provided increases in our social services, particularly larger payments to old age and blind pensioners and the other group I have talked about to-night, the widows of veterans of the last war, as well as the veterans themselves, of the last war and the present war.
Finally, with respect to the third part of our subamendment, evidence in support of which has already been given so well by other speakers of this group, we feel that the time has come to reverse the present trend in the direction of monopolistic control. We believe it is time we moved in the direction of more cooperative control, in the direction of the sharing by the people in the control of the economy of this country. In fact in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that we shall not have security in this land; we shall not play our part in making possible the century of the common man; we shall not achieve the things for which our people are fighting, until the control of the economy of this country is where it ought to be, in the hands of the common people, so that it may be made to serve their interests.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to follow closely the speech delivered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but I could not help thinking that his remarks were rather far removed from the facts when he said the people of this country individually were not sharing in the general wealth and prosperity of Canada more than at any other period in our history.
It has been my privilege to sit in this house for many years, but never have I heard a budget speech presented during a period more difficult than that through which we are now passing. As I listen to the socialistic speeches of hon. members to my left, and those of the hon. members to my right who form the right wing of the government of the day, when they speak about the things that are to come after the war and the problems we may have to face when our boys return, I wonder if we sometimes forget that we are a nation at war; that we are struggling with our backs to the wall' to save not only our own country but all civilization and freedom. We talk about the four freedoms that will flourish when peace returns; yet we hesitate and hazard the main freedom that is at stake in time of war. I

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
listened to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) give his side of the controversy with the premier of Quebec or the members of the legislature of that province as to the number of boats sunk in the St. Lawrence.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was not a controversy with the premier of Quebec.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman need not rise to interrupt me. The minister did not hesitate to deal with what was said by one who disagrees with him politically, but he was very careful not to repeat what was said by the premier of Quebec, who was absolutely in accord with the statements made in that province.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must correct my hon. friend. The premier of Quebec was not in accord with most of the remarks made by Mr. Gagnon.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He may not be in accord with most of the words that were uttered, but he was in accord with the kernel of what was said, that in the province of Quebec and along the St. Lawrence river there were all sorts of trouble of which the people were not aware.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did lie say so?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, he said so in the Quebec
legislature, as my hon. friend well knows.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
do not know that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not want to get into
any controversy, but wre might as well face the facts. We have been playing politics in this country all along the line.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), who applauds, should know better than anyone else, because no one plays politics more viciously than he does.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have the floor, Mr. Speaker. I do not interrupt my hon. friends when they make their political speeches; I do not interrupt the hon. member for Vancouver Centre who, though a minister of the crown, makes political speeches for the sake of the people of Vancouver. I am not trying to emphasize the number of boats that have been sunk in the St. Lawrence. The navy minister knows very well that I have not taken advantage of any information I may have obtained, that I have observed the etiquette which I believe an hon. member should observe in time of war.
I have not been in agreement with all that has been said, nor have I agreed with all the criticism in regard to boats sunk here or boats sunk there. I do not propose to tell Hitler anything if I can avoid doing so; I do not want to say that this boat was sunk at my back-door, or anything like that, but I do not intend to sit idly by and listen to a minister shield those of his own political faith while he tries to place the responsibility for everything upon the shoulders of those who normally are of a different brand of politics.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
am sure my hon. friend does not wish to be unfair, but the controversy between the Hon. Mr. Gagnon and myself arose as to the number of sinkings in the St. Lawrence. On that point the premier of Quebec made no statement whatever.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But he did with regard
to spies.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did not make any statement as to the number of ships sunk, but the Hon. Mr. Gagnon, a former colleague of my hon. friend1, did, and my hon. friend cannot escape responsibiilty now-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not trying to escape
responsibility, nor am I going to let the minister escape responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I
am not trying to. If your former colleague has the courage to come forward, we shall place the responsibility where it belongs.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to tell the minister
that I have as much courage as he has; that I was here before he was, and that I may be here after he leaves. Knowing the astuteness of those in this house who are so careful of those who support them, I was rather amused at the way in which Mr. Godbout, premier of Quebec, was carefully protected in regard to anything he said concerning German spies being in the province of Quebec, telling the boats where to land and so on, while Mr Gagnon was chastised in this house because he said there were more than thirty boats sunk instead of twenty. I did not intend to mention this matter to-night. I am not saying how many boats were sunk, because I do not know and evidently the minister does not know either.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, I do.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps Mr. Gagnon does not know; probably the premier of Quebec does not know. I mention this matter not to cause the minister any embarrassment but in order

The Budget-Mr. Rowe

to emphasize the fact that we are now passing through the most tragic, most difficult and most disastrous days Canada has ever experienced; yet during this debate we have heard hon. members to my left plead the cause of the fiddler at the Chateau Laurier and those to my right plead the cause of those who must have security without work when the war is over. All this time of war our boys are flying through dangerous mist and fog, fighting the battles to preserve our right to sit here. Surely it is time we stopped and looked at the signs which are apparent to us all. We are facing the most crucial days this nation has ever faced. This war has only begun. Why, Mr. Speaker, we have not won the battle of Africa ; we have not concluded the battle of the Mediterranean; we have not started into Europe. We failed to get into Dieppe and we boasted about getting out of Dunkirk.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We did not boast; we took justifiable pride in getting out.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, my hon. friend may take justifiable pride in being here representing Brantford City.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do indeed.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He may take justifiable pride in the fact that we got out of Dunkirk, but let us get down to the task that lies before us, the winning of this war. Let us forget about post-war problems for a moment. Let us win the war before we plan the peace. Let us plan for the boys who are fighting for us, while we are talking about some happy new form of security, something that may be used as a political catchword to appeal to the man on the street, something a little better than anyone has mentioned before.
I listened to the budget address with great interest. I have great admiration for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley).

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"Why?" somebody asks.
Because he is carrying a load my hon. friend may never carry; because he is trying to turn a people who are peace loving into a battling, fighting nation, to save this situation; because he is trying to raise five billions of dollars.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Five and a half.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, five and a half billions of dollars. Half a billion does not matter much, when you get into those figures. I remember when I came to this house first, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and the Hon.

Hugh Guthrie were trying to carry out their duties, and at that time the Prime. Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the late Mr. Lapointe and others stormed and fumed and worried when we got up to $400,000,000 in expenditures. But when we spend five and a half billion dollars, most of which is for fighting purposes, to save ourselves when we have our backs to the wall, not so much is said about it. In 1925 we would not have thought it possible.
I say the Minister of Finance has a gigantic problem. To him I give my utmost sympathy, and I give to him, as well, my cooperation; that is all he ever asks me for, and it is not a heavy burden on my part.
But, Mr. Speaker, I am amazed when I listen to the budget and realize the modesty with -which the budget impositions strike the people of Canada, and the tenseness with which news strikes the mothers of the boys who fight overseas. Oh, it is all very well to wipe fifty per cent off your income tax. It is all very well to say, We are not raising your taxes. It is all very well to have a budget which is lighter on the people than the budget of last year, despite the intensity of the war, the obligations which face us, and the task which lies before us greater than it ever was before. I am wondering whether it is the beginning of the end of this government. Surely the government would not plan an election budget in a time like this. If they have, then I want to compliment them upon having planned a very good one. I do not think they would be indulging in any such light gymnastics in a time of crisis. But it would take the cabinet working day and night for some time to think up a finer election budget than we have at the present time.
I will not go into details of it. However, I am rather amazed to find that our expenditures on civil and ordinary accounts are higher than they have ever been before- and at a time when they should have been lower. I realize that probably much of that increase might be correlated with indirect effects of the war. But when the people of Canada are struggling; when our people from the labouring man to the highly paid salary man are paying more income tax than any other people in the world, when we are facing a task such as we never faced before, then surely it is time we curtailed ordinary expenditures. Surely it is time we faced the task which lies before us. That task is the winning of the war.
No wonder our people are restless. No wonder they are discontented. No wonder they are worried whether we shall or whether

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
we shall not have an election. No doubt my hon. friends to my left will worry if we are to have one. Some of them will worry if we are not to have an election, because no doubt they can see the public growing more restless every day. And why are the people growing more restless? They are restless because, as I have said, we have in Canada the greatest national task which was ever placed before a Canadian people-and that greatest national task with the least possible planning. We have no plan. We have no plan for our armed forces. If the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) wishes to interrupt me I should like him to tell me if the government have sufficient reinforcements for this spearhead that they boast about, which will face the hun in Europe.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have no doubt we have sufficient reinforcements, and Canada will have no doubt about it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All I can say to my hon. friend is that he should be thankful to have such confidence with so little reason. Because surely my hon. friend, as a military man, knows that when there are not more than twelve per cent reinforcements in England for the Canadian corps to reinforce what will be the spearhead-surely there is nothing to boast about. The government have no military plan. They have no plan for production. The government know it, and so does every member of the cabinet. Probably that is why they are all out now, with the exception of one.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend has asked a question and he has answered it himself. He says that we have only twelve per cent reinforcements. All I will say is that he is incorrect, and that our reinforcements are ample, as he will soon learn.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if you will observe, that is a very vague answer. If I were not a farmer, and if I were a lawyer like him, I could make a better answer than that, because he does not give the number. I have found out from the very best military authority I can find, that we have less than ten per cent. I said twelve per cent so that I would not be lower.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would Hitler not like to know the truth?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: V es, and the people want to know that, too.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But Hitler-and I am not going to tell him.	.
72537-76i

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is the type of interjection from people who evidently know less about the matter than I know myself. They are not very impressive in the house, and less impressive to the mothers of the boys over there who will fight this battle.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why break down confidence?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not breaking down confidence. Why don't you build up confidence? Why don't you build up confidence, to have Canada know what you know as a military man, what is needed in this country, when we are facing the foe.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are building it up, in spite of what you are doing.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are building it up in
spite of what you are doing. You are building it up by the most haphazard, piece-quilted, slap-dash methods any government ever approached a problem. I am asking you: Can you tell me now what your man-power policy is? You cannot say what your agricultural policy is, or your military policy. The world knows it is the most hypocritical expression of Canadian sentiment we have ever known. Your government has started-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If
my hon. friend is asking me these questions I should be allowed to answer them. I cannot answer unless I am given the opportunity. I can assure him these questions will all be answered, but it will take more than just a sentence to answer them.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend wants to answer them by telling me they will be answered in due course by someone who can answer them better than he can. In its war policy and on its war plan the government has started too late. Our farmers produce at less than cost, but our manufacturers of munitions and supply produce at cost plus ten per cent.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not ten per cent.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. Some of them get
twenty per cent; some get twenty-five per cent and some get more.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us keep the record
straight.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If this answer is not any better than I have heard before, I shall have to use my own judgment to see whether it helps the record.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us keep the record
straight. My hon. friend does not suggest ten per cent, fifteen per cent, twenty per cent and twenty-five per cent? I know he does not
The Budget-Mr. Rowe

mean to suggest that. The profits on manufactured goods going into the war contracts are much less than that, and he knows it. There is no use in becoming hysterical about them.
