subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, I do not know that the minister has added a great deal. I assume the minister, realizing that I am a farmer, knows that no farmer in Canada has ten per cent. I was speaking on behalf of the farmers who hare worked longer for less than any other class of people in this country. Nobody knows better than he that friends of his government have received not only ten per cent, but some have received one hundred per cent in the last year or two.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Name one.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have not named anything yet to-night, so that you might as well keep your seat.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just in case silence may be thought to indicate consent, I wish to say that I now contradict that statement that my hon. friend has made.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go ahead; you have lots of time.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go on; let us have your speech.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about Churchill?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not speaking for
Churchill, and neither is Churchill speaking for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He spoke a word for Canada the other day.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is the first time I have seen the government setting up Mr. Churchill to speak for them. Talk about the sovereignty and independence of Canada! I want to say that following this war it will not be Churchill who will be held responsible; it will be the minister and the government. They are the people who will be held responsible. After nil, if we are thinking of this great Canada as an independent and sovereign state, we had better speak for ourselves and not rely on the haphazard complimentary laurels of Churchill or the facetiousness of Roosevelt. I realize that the government is quite glad at a time when they are a little doubtful about themselves to have a statement made such as the one Mr. Churchill made the other day. But I suggest that you cannot fight next year's battle with last year's requirements. We are facing the greatest battle that this country has ever faced.
VMr. McLarty.]
My hon. friend talks about how much the people have made in this war. I can take him through the country which he has not had the time to go through; I can take him into parts of my own district, and I think I can take him into parts of his own district and show him farmers who are paying three times as much for their labour to-day as they paid before the war. I can show him farmers who are making less money to-day than they made before the war. I can show him farmers whose little sons of fifteen and sixteen years of age are earning more money, working for men who have war contracts on a cost plus ten per cent basis, than their fathers on 150 acres of land.
Yet we speak of equality of service when there are provinces where thirty-two to thirty-nine per cent of the population have enlisted in the services as compared with nine and five per cent in other districts. Then we pull out the old bogey of national unity. You had better put alongside its old stablemate of equality of service. Let us face the facts. Let us face them as they should be faced by the Canadian people. Have you some mysterious formula by which you can encourage the farmers by patting them on the back, by saying they have been the backbone of Canada since confederation? Are we to tell the farmer, you are the type of man who will fight; you are the type of man who will work; you are the type of man who will toil from the early hours of the morning to the last dark hours of the night; you do not need a profit because of your love of service to the empire; you will do it anyway. Then you go down the line and you find a munitions manufacturer who has been given a cost-plus profit. We tell the farmer that we will select the men who will fix his prices; that we will make sure that none of his representatives is on the board; that we will fix prices so that when cattle are highest he will be encouraged to buy them, and then when we know that they are ready for market we will say they have dropped three and a half cents a pound. We will play to the consumers' market and we will tell them, we will give you a cost-of-living bonus.
This has been the most muddled policy that has ever been used in connection with any problem. What does our agricultural policy consist of? It is simply a conglomeration of ceiling prices and ration cards. It is simply telling the consumer, We are trying to make you buy less; we want you to eat less, and then telling the producer, We want you to produce more even though at less profit. I doubt if there is a member within sound of my voice, even the more socialistic members

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
to my left, who would attempt to condemn too vigorously the price ceiling. There are many who believe that there is some mythical or mysterious way in which we can maintain the solvency of Canada for the years to come.
I have grave doubts whether the panacea or the medical treatment we are being Gordonized with in this country is not worse than the disease itself. I cannot help thinking that the people whom this will help the most are those who will be clipping the most coupons in the years to come. I am not so sure but that the fear of inflation is causing more harm in this country than a degree of inflation itself. I see my hon. friend, the Minister of Agriculture, is here.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has been here all the time.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I knew he was here. I do not know whether he will agree with me. He seldom does-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is wise.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He is wise, my hon. friend says. I would not like to say what I might say. The minister is an astute politician but a poor agriculturist in times like this. I remember his speech in 1939 when he told us we would have plenty of pork, and now I observe his speeches when he says that there must be rationing. I remember when he said that we would have so much production that we would not know what to do with it, and now we have rationing. I remember when he bonused the farmers of western Canada not to grow wheat, to grow mixed grains instead. I recall also how he bonused the western farmers eight cents a bushel over the farmers of eastern Canada in order to enable them to produce mixed farm products at a profit in competition. Probably in the over-all performance it will serve a good end.
We talk about national unity; yet we practise all sorts of sectional policies. I am holding no brief against the farmers of western Canada because they have not as much as they might have, but I urge the Minister of Agriculture not to forget entirely that there are some farmers in eastern Canada, in Quebec and Ontario. The minister is two years behind with his agricultural policy. I remember saying to him when he was sitting in his own seat-I notice he is moving further back all the time-that this country would be faced with a food crisis before many years. I well recall when he came into this house first he laughed at me and said that western Canada would be the grain basket, the flour basket, or the bread basket of the world for years to come.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is still laughing at you.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes; he is still laughing at me, but he who laughs last laughs best. And your particular basket is so full it is running over, and now you have become accustomed to it running over, but you do not know what to do with the surplus wheat. You have produced more wheat, it is true, than we did in those years, but the fiasco of price ceilings as far as agriculture is concerned has been the joke of the North American continent. My hon. friends who sit to my left have talked since 1911 on the theme of dollar market prospects. I remember it coming up in 1911, at the first political meeting I ever attended. I drove a number of people to the meeting for my father, who saw a chance to defeat the Liberal government.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just go back to 1932 and tell us about that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Probably my hon. friend cannot go any further back than that, but I remember the speeches which were made in 1911, and how they pleaded with the farmers of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: "No truck or trade with the Yankees."

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock) was young at that time, and he is young yet. I remember how they talked at that time about what the farmers-of Canada would be able to do if the great markets of the United States of America were' opened up to them.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They were.
Mr. ROWE; They were, and they were closed to you so fast that it made you dizzy. They were closed in 1922, and again in 1928, and in 1929. My hon. friends pictured to the farmers all over this dominion what a great haven of possibilities the United States market would be, how you could sell your fat cattle from western Canada over there.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. ROWE; My hon. friend says "hear, hear". Yet you named a corporation recently when you had the market open to you, and under this policy, even though they want our stock, our feeding cattle and fat cattle will sell for three cents a pound less on Canadian markets than in the United States. Rather than let the farmer get that extra price, you establish a stabilization fund and buy the stock yourselves. What is the idea? Is the farmer of Canada the forgotten man?
The Budget-Mr. Rowe

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A year ago the hon. member was shouting about there being no beef in Toronto.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, I was, and since then there was no beef in Toronto.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was because it was going to the States.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you sent your representatives to buy beef, and I should like you to tell this house how much money they made on the beef they bought and how much they kept from the farmers of this country.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And what class of beef they bought.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, what type of beef they bought. There are scores of obvious reasons why the farmers of Canada are dissatisfied. There are scores of reasons which lead them to believe they are not only the forgotten men but the persecuted men of this war economy. I have heard a great deal of talk to the effect that farmers' sons are not engaging in this struggle, but I will venture to say that there is as great a percentage of farmers' sons fighting our battle overseas as any other class of the Canadian people.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Whoever said that farmers' sons were not taking part in the war?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is neither a farmer nor the son of a farmer, and I do not know why I should charge him with making a statement like that. He makes so many other statements which are inconsequential that I would not charge that one to him.
But our man-power planning has been a fiasco. It has been the monument of error of this government. Nobody knows that better than the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) whom I see across the floor. No wonder that Mr, Elliott Little, ex-chief of the selective service of this country, has quit. Who would not quit? I was amazed he stayed on as long as he did. Why should he be expected to stay to direct the man-power of Canada when the government for which he was working had no man-power policy? If they had a man-pow7er policy would they have let ten thousand men go over to the United States to find employment in the same kind of work in which our labour force was thirty per cent short in Canada?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member where those ten thousand men went.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows the answer so well that it would needlessly take

up my time and the time of the house to tell him. He has admitted that 3,500 went over, and he admitted there were others whom he did not know anything about.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If all the remarks of my hon. friend are as correct as that, there is not much to be said for his figures.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my remarks are no better
than the adequacy of the minister's labour policy, the house would be foolish to listen to me very long. The government have no labour policy. They have no man-power policy. There is a policy which says in effect, in one district we will call all the farmers up, but not in another district; if your boys are loyal and courageous enough to enlist and volunteer, we will take them whether the farmer is crippled or not. I have in my mail to-day-there is no use in handing it to the government because they must be swamped with such letters from all over the dominion- a letter from a man seventy years of age, with 200 acres of land. The hon. member for York North (Mr. Mulock) laughs, but I can tell the Postmaster General from what I know of the people of his constituency that he had better get back to York North and talk to the farmers if he expects ever to be returned to this house, because he knows very well that nobody has neglected their interests more than he has. They know that old farmers, tottering almost to the grave, have no other help than that of their wives and daughters. As a farmer wrote to me to-day, "I am seventy years of age; I was in bed for six months; my two sons are overseas; I have got a little girl thirteen years of age and my wife milking fourteen cows. Is there any chance of getting one of these boys back?" If we had a man-power policy; if we were facing this war courageously, facing it as a national problem, do you mean to tell me that we would not be able to let these boys know not only where they could not go but where they should go? I can tell my hon. friends of farmers in my own district who have four sons on 100 acres of land and none of the boys are in the war. What type of haphazard policy is this? How are you going to meet this crisis? We shall meet it if Russia stands for a while, and if old Britain and the United States of America, who have not hesitated, who have not rested on the laurels of a great production of guns and tanks and material things, but who have paid with their lifeblood for our glory, will continue to do so- we shall meet it then. But I shudder to think of what will happen if my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and my hon. friend the Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
National Defence (Mr. Ralston) are right in telling us that we are about to face the greatest battles which we have ever faced, and that our brave boys in Europe are to be the spearhead of this great and gallant task. If that is so, I say that the responsibility of having these boys assured before they go over the top that we have reinforcements behind them does not rest with the Churchill statement; it rests with the government of Canada; it rests with us, the parliament of Canada. Do not make any mistake about that. If, as the military people tell us, we are going to suffer casualties as high as seventy per cent, we shall hang our heads in shame if we find that we can replace them only to the extent of ten or twelve per cent. The hon. member for Brantford City says he knows the provision is ample, but he will not tell us the percentage.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He does not know.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If he says it is more than
ten per cent, I should like him to rise. If he says that it is twenty per cent, I should like him to rise. He will rise and nod his head in doubtful consent, but he does not know, for I have often seen him rise before when he did not know.
We have heard a great deal about all our post-war policies. I do not intend to deal further at this time with our agricultural problems. I should know something about agriculture. I do not know as much about it as I should, but even that is more than the hon. member for Brantford City professes to know except at election time.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have never set myself up as an agricultural expert.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should hope not from now on.
We have listened to a great deal of talk on post-war planning. As I listened, I thought of the farmers in my own district, and the same is true of many other districts in Canada, who are struggling to make a living and paying three times as much in wages as they were paying before the war, who are making no profits and have mortgages still hanging darkly over their heads, whose wives are working on the farm and wrecking their health, who themselves have to work so hard and long that many of them have to go to bed with a heart condition while their sons are fighting overseas. It is difficult for them to understand why the government places a ceiling price on what they have to sell and charges them three times as much for what they have to buy.
We have heard a great deal about post-war planning and a lot of social security dreaming. It is about time that we paused and started to study present-war planning rather than post-war security. It is about time that we hesitated to dream of security at a moment when this nation is on fire. There are plenty of post-war possibilities. Hon. gentlemen to my left say that the old order must go. Perhaps. But many brighter men than they are, thought that long ago. As I read history -I do not get much time to read it-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) has had more time to read history because he has left a lot of other things undone, but as I read history I recall that in 1782 William Pitt said that he saw nothing but ruin and depression in front of him. A little later on, Wilberforce said that he had met a girl whom he loved and would like to marry, but he never would while the future was so dark and uncertain. I recall that in 1839 Lord Elgin said that everything tended toward revolution and that in 1846 Disraeli saw no hope ahead for industry, commerce or agriculture. I recall that when Wellington was dying in 1852 he said that he was glad he was passing on before the ruin of depression gathered around him.
My hon. friends to my left have new ideas, but let me say to them that if we would only face the task that lies before us the future is not quite so dark. They have new plans. They want security so that those who are healthy will never be sick and those who are sick will be made well again, security for the people whether they want to work or not, security for those who even want to play as well as work. But let me say to them that under our present system of democracy, which is to disappear when their regime comes in-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have read your booklets and I realize that under your plans the whole present system must be changed. I even might expect to be working for some of those fellows in agriculture if their dreams came true. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that under our present system we have not done so badly. Let us look back to 1900. I do not give all the credit for what has happened since, to the Liberal party. After all, in their policies there has been some sense and soundness mingled with a lot of errors. Under our democratic form of government on the North American continent we have made progress
The Budget-Mr. Gauthier

since 1900, greater progress than has been made anywhere else. In 1900 only one out of a hundred on the North American continent hadi a buggy to drive. When this war started one out of five had an automobile.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They haven't now.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In 1900 our people had only eighty-six dollars per capita invested in life insurance; to-day they have $600 per capita, almost eight times as much. Therefore, I say to my hon. friends to the left, set about to improve the old system, or in better words of another, lop the mouldered branch away, before you attempt to cut down the tree that has sheltered you and under which you have prospered enough to be here, happy but discontented.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having just heard a speech in the language of Shakespeare, you will have no objection, I am sure, to my using for a few minutes Racine's idiom and affording thereby some rest to your ears.
Mr. Speaker, I have noticed in the speech from the throne that was read in the house- a speech on which we should have liked a vote to be taken although for one reason or another that has been impossible-that the government have taken election precautions probably to lessen the impact from the budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has recently introduced with such a high degree of courage. We note in the speech from the throne many precautionary measures intended for the electors not only of the dominion but especially of certain provinces, such as the appointment of a committee on post-war reconstruction and reestablishment, a national social security programme, including social insurance and even health insurance, which matters will all be investigated by committees whose work may not have been completed before the end of the session. Just the same, appearances shall have been kept up and if I may borrow a phrase from the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), a twig from the Christmas tree has even been included, as a scrap of comfort, when the 1938 dish was rehashed and the appointment of parliamentary secretaries was mentioned again. I realize that in order to make us swallow the budget recently introduced some kind of a sop was necessary and I also realize that, in view of the stand of certain provinces with Liberal leanings such as Saskatchewan and Ontario, which will soon have reached the end of the term of office, a chance had to be given to provincial followers, where, should the occasion arise, an election

would probably be held. As regards the province of Quebec, those who have read the speech from the throne know where they stand and in all probability the Liberal party in Quebec will sacrifice itself and will be the first to take the plunge in order to show to the dominion Liberal government how risky it is at this time to face the electors.
Much has been said about farmers' sons since the beginning of this session, and indeed since the outbreak of war. I remember that motions calling for the exemption of farmers' sons have either been ruled out of order or voted down by the majority.
I do not doubt for a moment the sincerity of the hon. members who derived great satisfaction from these motions being declared out of order nor their sincerity in voting against the motion calling for exemption in favour of farmers' sons, nevertheless, one may well -wonder if at the present time, had the government given more consideration to these requests in favour of farmers' sons, we would be facing such distressing problems concerning farm labour in Canada generally. Only last night, I heard the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) showing how the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) made contradictory statements, one to the effect that there need be no fear of any farm labour shortage while the other worried about this same shortage. One thing stands out, however, and that is a lack of cohesion, a lack of cooperation between the departments of government and I recall the speech made on March 24, 1942, in this house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), which appears on page 1562 of Hansard, which I quote:
The production of food in war time is one of the most essential tasks. To the extent that food is produced for Britain or other allied countries, or for Canada's own fighting men, it is a direct war service. If this aspect of Canada's total effort is not to suffer, the manpower required for food production must be kept available.
And I find on page 1567 that the Prime Minister also stated:
One of the man-power problems with which the country is faced is the growing shortage of agricultural labour.
What must we think, Mr. Speaker, of such statements? Everybody admits that thousands of farmers' sons are still in the army, that thousands of others had to remain there two, three, four and even six months, before being released. And during all that time farm work remained undone; those who did not have the money required for the hiring

The Budget-Mr. Gauthier
of hands had to leave their crops on the fields to spoil under the snow. A certain amount of wheat remained under the snow, as the hon. member for Bow River stated last night. An appropriate policy regarding farmers' sons would have prevented such a shortage of labour. I do not deny, Mr. Speaker, that it is honourable and praiseworthy to show as much courage and intrepidity as the farmers' sons who have enlisted voluntarily for Overseas service. On March 24, 1942, the Right Hon. Prime Minister stated, as reported on Hansard, page 1657:
Voluntary enlistment of farmers and agricultural workers in the army, the navy and air forces will continue to be encouraged. It is felt that the privilege of serving voluntarily in the armed forces should not be completely denied to a whole class of the community, however important may be the service its members are at present performing.
At different times, the government has announced, both in this house and in party newspapers, that farmers' sons would be exempted from military service, and the Prime Minister stated that voluntary enlistment of farmers' sons must be encouraged. I wonder, -and everyone is entitled to wonder-whether the government policy calls for leaving on the farms all the help needed. If agriculture ceases to produce, our soldiers overseas will have to go hungry. It is all very well to say that farmers' sons who have enlisted will be replaced by women, prisoners of war, Japanese or invalids. Even students have been put to work; such was the case last summer and such it will be again. But, Mr. Speaker, the farms need trained hands and nimble brains to accomplish the tasks necessary to produce all we need in a time of war not only for civilian consumers, but for the armed forces as well. In my opinion, the government's farm policy has proven wholly inadequate, completely lacking in both cooperation and coordination.
It may be thought that we too often dwell on this matter. Yet, we have every right to do so, indeed it is our duty to do so, since our repeated warnings to the government both inside and outside this house have ostensibly given them time to consider and adopt an adequate policy with respect to the people and the war effort.
Mr. Speaker, when a member of the Bloc Populaire or of any other opposition group from the province of Quebec rises to address this chamber, I understand how one might become fidgety and hark back to the example of France that owed her tragic fate to the large number of her political parties. I do not claim, neither have I the right to do so under
the rules of this house, that when the Prime Minister referred to the unduly large number of political parties in this country, he was merely trying to advance his own fortunes. I do not claim either that the Prime Minister views with alarm the establishment of opposition parties through which his personal desire to remain at the helm might find its Waterloo. The rules of the house prevent me from saying so. Anyone who asserts, giving France as an example, that the establishing of a large number of parties would be detrimental to the country, seems to be unfamiliar with history. Or could it be that the rise of too great a number of opposition groups from the province of Quebec is particularly irritating in certain quarters?
Anyone familiar with the causes of the downfall of France knows that her fate was not due to the multiplicity of her political parties but' rather to the manifold international interests which weakened her and prevented Germany from paying off the full amount of the reparations due; which allowed the demilitarisation of the Ruhr and subsidized the electoral campaigns of certain French politicians. These, and not the unduly large number of her political parties really brought about the downfall of France. Any comparison between France and Canada must needs be unsatisfactory. I repeat there is a pretense at being unfamiliar with international history.
The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) made an inquiry regarding a resolution which came to me from the city of Three Rivers. If I may refer to the subject, without incurring the hon. member's displeasure, the resolution reads as follows:
To the Right Honourable William Lyon
Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Whereas the present butter ration is wholly inadequate to the war worker who takes his lunch to the factory; and
Whereas such ration, in addition to being inadequate, is calculated to cause serious prejudice to the worker's war effort; and
Whereas so harsh a measure obviously discriminates between those who are in a position to abide by it and others which it too severely affects;
Be it therefore resolved that the dominion government be respectfully requested to do everything in its power to improve the untenable situation in which the Canadian worker now finds himself through the action of the wartime prices and trade board, and to impress upon the board the urgency of giving full priority to the needs of our workers engaged in this country's war production by requesting that they increase the ration of essential commodities granted these men, particularly their butter ration.
The Budget-Mr. Gauthier

This resolution, Mr. Speaker, is selfexplanatory. And notwithstanding the reply given this afternoon to the hon. member for Gaspe, I cannot understand that the workers, whether employed in our war plants or in our mines, at any rate, all those who must carry their meals with them, who have no time to return to 'their homes either at noon or in the evening, these need a more substantial butter ration than office workers who take their meals at home or in a restaurant.
I hope that the provincial treasurer and the government will reconsider this decision and that employees of all classes will be allowed more butter for their meals.
The sinking of ships in both the river and the gulf of St. Lawrence has been the cause of quite a controversy. It is neither my duty nor my intention to stand in this house for the member for Matane, the hon. Mr. Gagnon nor is it my intention to take the defence of the provincial government; far from it. It does seem to me, however, that this government should have listened to the claims and the warnings, though mild they may have been, that we have expressed in this house and elsewhere since 1937. They should also have devoted their attention primarily to the defence of this country. I admit that different theories have been expounded in this house to the effect that we should go to meet the enemy wherever he may be rather than have him attack our shores. To this I have replied recently that the same principle applies to all countries and not only to Canada. I understand also that the government only acted under pressure from total-war men since the start of the war. I also fully realize that they may have somewhat forgotten to give the St. Lawrence gulf and even the river the appropriate defence they deserved. It was, however, most important that they send soldiers overseas. That was urgent. Food had also to be sent. I have shown, a few moments ago, that not only had they forgotten steps to defend the country and the St. Lawrence shores, but they had ignored agriculture as well. This controversy had originated from statements made by two members of the Quebec legislature which had been referred to in this house. I am not concerned with the number of ships sunk either in the gulf or St. Lawrence river, but one thing is certain-I say it without any intention of giving out information that may be helpful to the enemy-if adequate defence works had been provided, if the government had been interested first of all in the defence of our country, we would not have to- announce sinkings in the gulf and St. Lawrence river.

Indeed, those who are conversant with existing conditions, who know where enemy ships and submarines enter, also know that protection against the entry of these enemy ships would be a relatively easy matter.
Mr. Speaker, while discussing the increase in military appropriations, in 1937-

speechtext: The hon. member's friends, for their part, cast their votes for the national defence appropriations.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have voted in favour of a number of appropriations, while insisting that others be decreased, because, as we stated, the government policy was not merely concerned with the defence of Canada, but with that of the empire at large. In support of our claims we referred to a statement of Hore-Belisha who, at a banquet held in London, at that time had said that a colonial defence policy could not be considered within the empire, but that the defence of the empire should come first. The hon. member must remember this.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And since that time he has been out of the cabinet.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does not matter whether he has left the cabinet or not. There are so many who wish to enter it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is why my hon. friend now sits on the other side of the house.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I never asked or expected it. I am here because I am not like my hon. friend who has broken his pledges and his word.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is impossible!

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope my hon. friend will keep quiet.
In 1938 and 1939 we have raised the same objections, always urging the government to give particular attention to the defence of our country. We were then against participation in outside wars. On account of that stand, we were well supported by our electors in the by-elections of 1937 and 1938, and we have enjoyed such support for twenty years, as my hon. friend from Chambly-Rouville no doubt remembers. We were not campaigning alone, we had the help of men who were eloquent

The Budget-Mr. Gauthier
speakers, we were helped by outstanding men whose views were similar to our own. Conditions have changed, we were told, when we spoke against participation. We are told, in this house one year after: How can we participate in a war and do it on a moderate scale? That is the only consideration we have received for having believed what we were told. Mr. Speaker, we have to a certain extent accepted participation in outside wars but under the solemn pledge that conscription would never be enforced in this country. However, the government had a conscription act passed last year.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has not yet been enforced.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let my hon. friend be patient.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I say that it has not been enforced.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend were willing to look into the situation he would find that a 25-year-old physician, who is a married man has been called for military service under the National Resources Mobilization Act; the only thing this young physician can do is either to serve as a private within the country under the Mobilization Act or to volunteer, for overseas service. That is a splendid voluntary system. I could mention, as I have already done in this house, some of the means to which- the government have resorted in order to obtain the men they need to bring the army up to strength.
I am glad my honourable friend interrupted me. He has reminded me of something. When I voted for the National Resources Mobilization Act, I thought that the government intended to use it merely to call up men for service within this countiy, but I found out the other day, during the debate on the subamendment moved by the honourable member for Richelieu-Vercheres that the government had another objective and another intention. In reply to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres the Prime Minister had this to say in connection with the suspension of the Mobilization Act. I quote from page 558 of Hansard, February 19, 1943:
Those men who are a long distance from home, who are helping to protect this country and to save it from disaster, would be asking themselves: Is this the kind of support we are getting from our country and from our government? Is our parliament going to support that kind of action? Does it mean that while we are fighting here we are not going to get the reinforcements that we had hoped would he ready to come, if they were necessary?
In what manner would suspension of the Mobilization Act hinder reinforcements going
to our active army if that act had applied to service in this country only?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow me-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let my hon. friend not interrupt.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, I will answer him immediately.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I ask my hon. friend-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the hon. member afraid?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When the Prime Minister in reply to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) said: "Where will those men get reinforcements if we suspend the operation of the National Resources Mobilization Act?"

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend does not wish me to answer?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One minute. What impatience! How can you say that the Mobilization Act was for service only in this country when it was the intention of the government to reinforce the depleted ranks abroad. A mobilization act for this country, for this country only, and intended to fill the gaps in an army overseas. Such is the measure of voluntary enlistment favoured by the government according to the Prime Minister's own words in this house.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Draftees allow those who have voluntarily enlisted to go overseas. They take their place. That is the situation.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that all that the hon. member has to offer for an answer?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I put a case to the hon. member just now. He made no reply. I will give you another method, besides that of the Mobilization Act as adopted by this house, used for compelling our citizens into overseas service. The heads of families seeking employment in the different departments must obtain a release from the army. Such is the voluntary system. What does the hon. member think when he says: Wait, the measure is not yet in force? My hon. friend comes from Montreal and I see other hon. members who also come from Montreal. I have yet to hear any protest voiced regarding the port of Montreal, but last year that port and the St. Lawrence river were almost empty of ships.
I humbly submit that an adequate coastal defence would have facilitated traffic up the St. Lawrence and the bringing up of supplies to the port of Montreal, whereas part of that
The Budget-Mr. Gauthier

harbour's business is being carried by rail to eastern ports. I am waiting to hear any protests from the hon. member on this point.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Had the Bloc Populaire voted for that in 1937, the harbour of Montreal would be better protected.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let my hon. friend possess his soul in patience. He will feel the Bloc sooner than he expects.
I enquired the other day, Mr. Speaker, about broadcasts and put the following question to the government:
Is the dominion government responsible for, or author of the sketch "Our Canada" broadcast over the French network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation?
And the government replied:
"Our Canada" is a programme of the national war finance committee broadcast over a French network.
While listening to that programme one evening, I realized that the government, as stated in the fourth answer, besides giving a translation of Colin Ross' book, had seized the opportunity to advertise the speeches of the Prime Minister. The sponsor said before the opening of the programme: "It is an absolute truth which we must swallow if we are to be immune from dangerous suggestions, as our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated last week in the House of Commons when he said that he did not think that we can too strongly dwell on the gravity of the present situation and on the effort we shall be called upon to make. He wished to caution the people of Canada and the members of parliament against such a thought, and added that it would be dangerous to believe that the war can be won this year as no attempt had yet been made at invasion of the continent."
And a few minutes later, in the programme "Notre Canada", some noted and talented actors were reporting that the continent had been invaded and that the Germans were having trouble with the people of a certain village.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is himself making propaganda in favour of the government.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like hon. members to be a little more polite.

speechtext: Order! I would ask the hon. member for Portneuf to restrain his language.

speechtext: The hon. member is making propaganda in favour of the Liberal government.	.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF TIIE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the government to use a little more tact in outlining its policies and to refrain from spending public funds on government propaganda, although I do not mean to object to war propaganda as part of the government's policy.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I again refer to the creation and existence of several political parties in Canada and I know that our people, not only in the province of Quebec but in the whole of Canada will, at the proper time and place, recognize on the one hand those who have been frank, who kept their word, showed themselves honourable men, honourable statesmen and kept their pledges to the taxpayers and, on the other hand, those who miserably and woefully failed to do so.
